item.title: Opposing AI For the Wrong Reason
item.description: I’m pretty worried about how AI might impact the future.
item.content:encoded:
I’m queasy about how AI might impact the future. This technology is on track to have unprecedented power, and I think we should think meticulously about what we do with it and how we develop it. Luckily I feel the zeitgeist turning towards realizing some of the potential dangers of AI. Let’s see what the people are saying.

Oh.

Oh…1

Ah…

Were dead, he would be spinning in his grave. Luckily he is not, and so I can only assume he is simply spinning.

AI is on track to become a tremendously powerful technology, and there is a decent chance that it will completely change the world in the not too distant future.2 Maybe it isn’t too likely that it’ll kill us all—though we should seriously consider the possibility—but any technological change on this scale is bound to be riddled with risks. Yet it doesn’t seem like many people are really thinking seriously about how we best navigate these developments.

So I was tentatively hopeful when I started to see worries about AI spreading, both online and in real flesh-and-blood life. Maybe AI risks will become part of the political agenda—the stuff to decide elections. Maybe these are the first steps to slowing down a little, while we get an idea of what is going on. Maybe…

But no. What people are latching onto is the water issue (which is fake), the way AI is stealing jobs (and art) from artists, and how annoying Gemini search results are. I mean, maybe some of these are genuine issues—I’m generally skeptical—but they’re decidedly not the stuff we should be most worried about! Whether or not speaking with ChatGPT is as evil as drinking a glass of water is simply peanuts compared to preparing for what might be the biggest and fastest technological revolution ever!

As someone who has spent unreasonable amounts of time thinking about mereology, I shouldn’t be talking if my complaint were simply that people are wasting time talking about trivial issues. That’s not my problem though. My problem is that, although people worried about X-risk and power concentration agree with those focused on AI’s environmental costs that AI may be harmful, the two positions reflect fundamentally different attitudes toward the technology.

It’s hard to think that the biggest problem with AI is its water use, unless you also think that it’s useless. You have to think that LLMs are novelties, not worth the water you use in a second of showering.3 With this attitude you will never worry about AI takeovers, because “stochastic parrots” cannot take over anything. I see this all the time—there is no critique of AI’s environmental impact without the word “slop” being uttered in the same breath. But while AI is supposedly incompetent, many of the same people will quickly turn around to berate anyone using it.

There’s a bit of a tension in this. Like with Schrödinger’s immigrant who both steals your job and free-rides on welfare handouts, Schrödinger’s AI is simultaneously stealing artists’ and writers’ jobs and too dumb and useless to create anything of value.

If I were more uncharitable, I’d say it’s because we’re all scared.4 We’ve all seen the transition from incoherent Italian brainrot videos to people seriously debating in the comments whether or not a video is AI-generated—all within a year. We’ve all seen flaw after flaw in ChatGPT get fixed. But in the face of this, we decide to slide down different sides of the horseshoe.

Going down one side, you start listening to doom debates, fantasizing about Eliezer Yudkowsky reading your LessWrong posts, and donate your life savings to the EA Long-Term Future Fund. However, going down the other side, you can’t handle the idea that AI might make most current types of human intellectual labor obsolete, and so you decide that it can’t; it actually only ever produces stupid slop—oh and btw it is using all of our water. That’s what I’d say if I were more uncharitable.

But shouldn’t I just be happy that the two sides of the horseshoe are kissing at the bottom? Who cares why people oppose the rapid and reckless development of AI, so long as they do? I hope so. Yet I’m skeptical.

The problem is that the attitude that makes you complain about water use and RAM prices will not give any interest in preventing risks premised on AI being transformative. Maybe there will be some minor overlaps in opinion, but when it actually comes to investing considerable effort and resources in mitigating these risks, we will part ways.

Dedicating your life to prepare for the revolution Segways would bring to our infrastructure would have been a waste of time. And if your biggest gripe with AI is that you have to scroll 0.5 seconds extra to get to your search results, then you will not go out of your way to prepare for its transformative impact.

In fact, I worry that it’s worse than nothing. If seeing AI as a wasteful next token-predictor with no potential becomes an ingrained part of your attitude towards the technology, you’ll probably be less prone to take risks seriously than someone with no opinion.

Okay, this was more unstructured polemic than what I usually do, but it’s something that’s been bothering me for a while. Rant over.

An AI could never write an authentic Wonder and Aporia post.

item.title: All Religions or No Religions
item.content:encoded:
1In light of the recent miracle discourse on this platform [editors note: not recent anymore], I’ve been thinking about religion. Specifically, I’ve been thinking about whether I should convert to Catholicism. The answer I’ve come to is no. Not just because I don’t find the miracle claims unpersuasive (I’m sort of undecided on that), but because I don’t think that Catholicism being true is the best explanation of the miracles in question being veridical.

Instead I think that we should either believe all religions or no religions. Atheists should obviously agree with this (ignoring atheistic religions for a second). But even if God exists, I either think no religions are correct or all religions are correct.

My aim here will then be to present the disjunction of religious pluralism and religious… nihilism(?), as a master-hypothesis that always wins—showing that you certainly shouldn’t be an exclusivist, and take some particular religion to be correct.

The Hypothesis

Let’s first get clear on what the hypothesis I’m defending is. Basically, it’s this:

All or Nothing (AoN): Either all religions are correct, or no religions are correct.

The only alternative to this is, obviously, that some but not all religions are correct, and the most salient version of this is that only one religion is correct.

While this definition is reasonably clear, there are at least two points that need clarifying.

Correctness

When I say that a religion is correct, what exactly do I mean here? Clearly not that all claims of all religions are true—unless I want to embrace a version of dialetheism that would make Graham Priest have a heart attack.

Instead, I have to mean something softer. It’s hard to spell this out precisely, but the idea is roughly that a religion is correct if it is somehow “endorsed” by God, or “gets at” the truth. This is maybe not much more helpful than where we were two seconds ago, but I hope you can somewhat follow what I mean. Basically, it’s not necessarily about religions endorsing true propositions, but religions being viable ways of coming “in contact” with the divine.

Perhaps a more philosophical sounding way of putting it is that religion X is correct iff, had God or some other divine entity not intervened in the world or ordained the world with X in mind, then X would not have existed (or it would have been radically different). This doesn’t quite capture atheistic religions, and for these we’ll probably just have to resort to the idea of “getting at” the truth.

Again, this won’t be winning any conceptual-clarity awards, but I hope it’s enough for you to grok what I’m gesturing at.

All Religions

As stated here, “all religions” is ambiguous between rigidly designating all current religions, and flaccidly designating any religions that exist whatever they turn out to be. This point looks a little nitpicky, but it’ll be important once we evaluate the prior in a minute. And well, I mean to flaccidly designate all religions, not rigidly designate them.

While we’re here, I’ll also just add a small qualification: “Religion” is vague, and I won’t put it past humans to have come up with something we might recognizably call a religion, but which doesn’t have God’s stamp of approval. So by all religions I just mean all reasonably large ones—certainly all world religions.

The Prior Probability

We’ll then proceed in two steps: First we’ll look at how plausible the AoN hypothesis is prior to looking at the world, and then we’ll look a little at what the world is like, and see how that should change our assessments.

I think it’ll be a good idea to divide our assessment of AoN into two parts: Given theism and given atheism. The given atheism part is pretty close to trivial, since you’ll hold that no religions are correct, barring atheistic religions—actually it almost just follows from how I defined “correct.” For this reason I’ll also not really focus on the atheistic side throughout this post. Suffice it to say that if you’re an atheist—and certainly if you’re a naturalist—you should accept AoN because you should accept the “no religions are correct” disjunct.

Things are more interesting, and trickier, when we look at the theism side. Here it’ll be fruitful to return to the point about rigid designation. If AoN rigidly designated all current/historical religions, the “all religions are correct” part would be extremely low in prior. There are just so many random religions out there, that it’d be super unlikely that the ones that have happened to spring up throughout history should be correct.

So of course we’ll flaccidly designate all religions, whatever they are. To be fair to the exclusivist hypothesis, we’ll then also start by comparing to a flaccid version of this. That is, we compare the two hypotheses: 1) “Either all religions are correct or all are incorrect,” and 2) “some but not all religions are correct.” And perhaps specifically comparing (1) with: 3) “one religion is correct.” And all of these are flaccid, not referring to any particular religions.

The question we have to ask ourselves then becomes whether we should expect God to make all religions true or false, or whether he would want to prioritize particular religions. To make anything resembling plausible judgments, I’ll allow myself to put a couple of things in the background here, namely general knowledge about what humans are like, as well as general knowledge about what religions are like.

When we do this, it seems to me that the balance ends up pointing a little towards AoN over exclusivism, for a couple of reasons. First, if we assume that God wants to be “in contact” with his creation, there are the facts that:

  • Humans differ a lot in temperament, and in how they best come in contact with the divine. Some are comfortable in the free-flowing milieu of charismatic Christianity; some more so in the rigid rule-based structure of Catholicism or conservative Islam; still some in the contemplative nature of many eastern religions. Hence it would make sense for God to allow humans to create the religious structures that best fit them, and allowing them to come in contact with him through these.

  • Religions are quite geographically limited. So if God loves the whole world, it’d be a strange choice to choose a single one to be the correct one, effectively limiting his ability to have a relation with his creation.

  • In line with this, there is also just a basic consideration about fairness. It seems somewhat cruel or unfair for God to simply endorse certain religions, and not others, leading people who are trying their best to contact him astray through no fault of their own. All religions being correct and all religions being incorrect both seem a lot fairer than some religions being correct, but not others.

  • On the other hand, maybe God wants to communicate certain doctrines or truths clearly, which a single religion might lend itself better to (we’ll get to that below).

If God is more deistic in nature, not wanting to contact his creation, then AoN just wins outright, as we would then clearly expect no religions to be correct, rather than some.

Hence I think AoN starts out with a pretty sizable advantage over exclusivism, at least when we stick to flaccid versions. And I actually don’t think things change much when we make exclusivism rigid, designating some particular religion (presumably the most plausible one). It’ll lose a lot of prior probability, but at the same time it’ll gain a lot of predictive power, and so we just move the plausibility around, not really changing it. The same could be said for making AoN rigid to designate all religions that will have existed—but it’s easier to think about it in the flaccid version, so we’ll stick to that.

The Evidence

So before looking at the world, it seems that AoN has a decent advantage over exclusivism. That’s all well and good, but if AoN is beaten out by exclusivism on the empirical evidence, then that’s still bad news. Therefore we turn to that.

Miracles

The muse of this post (one might even say the ) was the recent discussion of miracles on phil Substack—especially Catholic miracles, and especially especially the Miracle of the Sun.

And I’ll just be upfront: It does seem to me like miracles point towards exclusivism of Christianity being correct (perhaps Catholicism specifically). That said I think there are a few things we can say to weaken the blow.

But just getting the facts on the table, there are quite a few reasonably plausible miracle reports within Catholicism, e.g.:

  • The Healings at Lourdes

  • The Miracle of the Sun

  • Potentially some eucharistic miracles.

And also just within Christianity more broadly (especially Charismatic kinds) there are frequent reports of healings (e.g. 62% of U.S. Pentecostals and 29% of all U.S. people claim to have witnessed/experienced a divine healing).

For other religions, things are a little thinner. I’ve had a harder time finding numbers on how many people report having miraculous experiences within other religions. But if we just look at the most prominent cases, things seem to look worse:

  • In Islam the main miracles are ones reported in the Hadith, which, suffice it to say, isn’t quite the evidential rigor of most prominent Christian miracles. On top of this there are purported prophecies and scientific predictions.

  • In Hinduism there are many stories of siddhas with supernatural powers, though these are mostly anecdotal without independent attestation. There was also a phenomenon in 1995 of Ganesha-statues drinking milk, but that was explainable with capillary action.

  • Perhaps the strongest non-Christian case is the execution of the Báb in 1850. Here the leader/founder of Bábism was shot at by a firing squad. After the smoke cleared the Báb was missing and back in his room unscathed. I haven’t looked into it too much, but it seems quite well-attested by independent sources both sympathetic and skeptical. However, he was then shot dead on the second round which is a bit strange for a miracle. And besides, the Baháʼí Faith (basically the modern version of Bábism) is a quite small religion (7-8 million followers) which would make it a strange candidate for a big competitor to Christianity.2

Looking at this evidence, I think it’s clear that miracles seem to point quite strongly towards Christianity, and perhaps specifically to Catholicism. That being said, I think there are a couple of things we can say in the other direction.

First, as a general point, it’s important to note that for Christian or Catholic exclusionists (or well for exclusionists of any sorts) any plausible miracles outside of their religion will be evidence against their view. This is particularly important because once you start accepting hypotheses/mechanisms for accounting for miracles in other religions, you also have to point those towards your own miracles and see whether they survive. So there is both a kind of cancelling out of the evidence, and a undercutting of it. That being said, if one religion has notably stronger miracle claims—as is plausibly the case—then the balance of the evidence will obviously still be in favor of exclusivism.

Second, as mentioned, Protestant Christian miracle claims are quite widespread, including some reasonably well-attested ones like the healing of Barbara Snyder. Now, Catholicism and Protestantism have some pretty deep disagreements, so this will to some extent have a “cancelling out” effect as described above. Though it might just be considered evidence for some sort of “mere Christianity.”

Third—and perhaps most important—there are plausible debunking accounts for why you would see this kind of distribution of miracles, which fit well with AoN. There are certain features of various religions which make what we see expected, even if God doesn’t favor one religion over another.

For instance, Catholicism has institutions in place with clear rules for checking and verifying miracle claims. Hence it makes sense that we would see the most thoroughly attested and scrutinized miracles in Catholicism.

Similarly Charismatic Protestantism puts weight on a personal relation with God, and “decentralized” spirituality. And what do we find? Many disparate and anecdotal miracle claims.

In Hinduism miracles don’t serve the same function of “verifying” the religion as in Christianity—rather they serve more to inspire and promote devotion. And this fits well with the pattern of anecdotal miracles centered around saint-like figures.

In Islam miracles are viewed mainly as vindication of prophets—not seen as communication between God and ordinary believers. And again, this fits well with the fact that the main miracle claims center around Muhammed and the Quran.

These are obviously broad strokes, and there are nuances and differences among branches of these religions. But the main point stands: The distribution of miracles fits well with the “characters” of the different religions. This debunks the evidence for exclusivism to some extent, as it makes the distribution of miracles more expected on AoN:

  • It makes it more expected if no religions are true. If no religions are true, there is some naturalistic explanation for apparent miracles. And whatever it is, these differences between religions would create selection effects to generate the distribution we see, even if we assume an equal baseline of miracle-like-events between religions: If a miracle-like-event happens in Catholicism it’ll be scrutinized and documented, if it happens in Islam it’ll be downplayed and more unnoticed as people aren’t looking for it among non-prophets, etc.

  • It also make it more expected if all religions are true. The above obviously still holds, assuming an equal baseline. But even if selection effects aren’t enough there is the point mentioned in the prior section (the Prior-section): We would expect God to make religions fit with different types of people given pluralism. And the kind of person attracted to Catholicism would need well-documented miracles in a way that a person attracted to Buddhism wouldn’t. Hence what we see makes sense.

Having made all these points, though, I won’t try to run from the fact that the distribution of miracles does point towards exclusivism.

Morality

Now that we’ve given exclusivism its due, we turn to the main thing that makes it implausible for me: Most religions—and especially the ones most favored by miracles—have incredibly implausible moral commitments.

The obvious place to start here is Catholicism. Catholicism commits you to believing that:

  1. Lying is always wrong.

  2. Sex outside of marriage is wrong.

  3. The use of contraception is wrong.

  4. Homosexual acts are wrong.

  5. Human life begins at conception and abortion is wrong.

  6. Women may not be ordained.

With perhaps the exception of 5, all of these are extremely obviously false! Like Moorean-truth level obvious! Unless you’ve been raised or coaxed into believing these, I can’t see how you would find these plausible at all!

Things are of course a little looser for Protestants, as they don’t have papal authority. Though they do have sola scriptura and many are inerrantists. This ostensibly leads them to having to accept 2, 4, and 6 above. There is also on the face of it support for ETERNAL CONSCIOUS FUCKING TORMENT in the Bible (though people will disagree a lot here). The Old Testament also appears to endorse widespread conquest and killing, as well as death-sentence for adultery, cursing your parents, and being a rebellious child. All of the passages in question are of course open to interpretation to greater or lesser extent, and one could go an errantist route. But all of this will involve epicycles and make your view take a hit.

Islam is no better off here, with whipping or stoning for adultery, a lot of sexism including polygyny, harsh penalties for homosexuality, etc. I don’t know too much about Hinduism, but it does appear to endorse hierarchies based on caste, animal sacrifice, and good ol’ sexism (as with most religions).

If you’re an exclusivist you have to reckon with this for some religion. One option is to try to explain away why you won’t have to accept these moral judgements. Mileage will vary between religions here as to how easy this will be, but it will be quite costly no matter what it seems.

You could of course also try to just accept the weird moral judgements. Things look even worse here, though. To do this you not only just face the fact that you have to accept some very implausible claims. On top of this you’ll almost surely have to revise your moral epistemology to make sense of this, as you can no longer trust moral intuitions. But as I’ve explained before, this wreaks havoc on the ability to argue for theism: To make predictions on theism we rely on having a good grasp of what is good, as God is supposed to do what is good. But once we give up on having an immediate idea of what is good, instead making it dependent on God, we end up having all kinds of skeptical scenarios where morality is completely different, but God deceives us—and we lose the ability to predict what God would do.

On the other hand AoN accommodates all of this very well. If all religions are correct to some extent, but also flawed (as they’ll have to be, since they can’t all be completely true at the same time), then it makes perfect sense that they would get some things right, when morally ignorant people constructed them—but they can be improved over time. Likewise if all religions are incorrect.

Strange Claims

This is really just an expansion of the above. But religions don’t just have many strange moral claims, but also many strange claims in general. For instance:

  • God is a trinity: Three persons that are identical to God but not identical to each other. Certainly doesn’t work with the definition of “=” in predicate logic, lol. (Christianity)

  • Jesus is fully human and fully divine. (Christianity)

  • Martyrs will get 72 virgins in heaven. (Islam)

  • Enlightened beings being able to be at several places at once (Mahayana Buddhism)

On top of this, with book-based religions like Christianity and Islam, you have the further headache of trying to harmonize apparently contradictory texts.

The point here is more general, though: A religion commits you to accepting a lot of things, and often many of these things are hard to defend. Thus exclusivism takes a big hit. For the same reasons as outlined above, AoN can better accommodate this.

Consensus

One last point, which I’ve labeled “consensus” (as you can see), is a consideration of the popularity and distribution of religions.

Looking at common consensus, some religions (especially Christianity, Islam, and Hinduism) stand out as prime candidates for exclusivist religions. Not only is consensus generally a good epistemic guide, but if God endorses a religion, he’d presumably want a lot of people to believe it, and so the true religion had better be one of the popular ones.

But the pluralist position has even stronger consensus in one sense: 75% of people subscribe to some religion, which is much better than any particular religion. Hence it seems that consensus favors pluralism.

There is of course a way of looking at it that points in the complete opposite direction: Almost no one accepts all religions—that is, almost no one is a pluralist. But at this point we have to be careful to remember why consensus is a good epistemic guide: Because groups are generally reliable on a lot of topics. Consensus doesn’t magically confer justification—it gives justification when you expect that people are better than random. But if pluralism is true, we’d expect a lot of people to believe that they have the correct religions, being geographically clumped—basically everything we observe. One is tempted to bring up the image of blind people feeling an elephant, but I’ll spare your eyes.

We have to be careful not to double-count evidence here. We already accounted for general facts about the geographical distribution and whatnot of religions when we looked at the priors. So at worst there’s nothing here, and at best pluralism gets a pretty significant boost. Either way exclusivism is definitely not scoring any wins on this point.

As for if all religions are false, then I think there’s some evidence against this in so many people being religious. But once you accept that there is some naturalistic explanation for how religions form (as there are plausible candidates of) then what we see actually fits quite well with no religions being true, and so the evidential weight here is lukewarm either way.

Conclusion

So there you have it. I think this case is pretty strong. Not in the sense that it’s a slam dunk P(AoN)=0.99 type deal. Rather I think the strength is in the case relying on very broad features that make it hard for me to see how exclusivism is going to claw its way up to being more plausible. Unless miracles for one religion turn out to be many times more compelling than for other religions, on top of plausible moral teachings, plausible descriptive claims, and wide following, I just don’t see any religion beating out AoN. And well… that’s not what we observe.

So which disjunct of AoN do I think is more likely? Obviously, if God doesn’t exist then the no religions part. But if God does exist I probably lean somewhat towards religious pluralism. Though evil, as well as naturalistic explanations for the occurrence of religions, etc. does pull in the direction of some sort of deism. Really, it’s probably gonna come down to the strength of miracle claims.

For what it’s worth I consider myself a Christian. Obviously not in the exclusivist sense, but in the sense that if pluralism is true, it’s one way to connect with God. And, well, it’s the way I’ve grown up with, one that fits my culture, one where I can get behind many of the values (other than the things mentioned here), etc. And if all religions are false, then what’s the harm?

What’s the harm in subscribing to Wonder and Aporia?

item.title: There's No Hand-Holding in Ethics
item.content:encoded:
I.

Inside each of us lives a beast that yearns to be told what to do. What do I have to achieve in order to have done my part? What is the right thing to do? The ostensible purpose of ethics is to feed this beast. Upon closer scrutiny, it becomes increasingly clear that nothing can ever satisfy it.

Perhaps if all ethics demanded of us was that we don’t do anything actively bad, it could succeed. So long as the world wouldn’t be a better place if you held your breath and keeled over, you’ve done your part. Trouble is that this is not enough. A life lived with the goal of never treading on anyone’s toes is a failure, because anyone well-off enough to be reading this also has a duty to help others.

Anyone clever enough to read this blog will have heard of Singer’s drowning child thought experiment. If you come upon a child drowning in a pond, you ought to save it. Always looking the other way in the face of beings’ suffering is perhaps not worse than nothing, but it is worse than what can be expected of any minimally decent human.

II.

The problem is that our duty of beneficence knows no bounds. At least, it knows no definite bounds. When as soon as duties go from being negative duties of avoiding harm to positive duties of promoting the good, there is no longer any principled place to stop. Should I donate $10 to the local homeless shelter? Should I spend my evenings ladling soup? Should I quit my job for a higher earning one to save the next marginal shrimp?

With negative duties, the line is quite clear: Don’t do anything actively harmful, and you’re in the clear. If your goal is to avoid causing harm, you can literally do no better than nothing, and so you should simply stop there. But with positive beneficence, the only thing you cannot surpass is absolute perfection, and we’d hardly want that as the bar to clear.

Maybe that’s a little too quick. The fact that a theory is difficult to follow does not automatically show it to be wrong—it only shows us to be acting wrong. But the problem isn’t so much that the bar of perfection is unreachable as that it misses the point.

There is no categorical difference between doing your best and doing your second-best. For negative duties there is a clear difference between doing nothing and doing almost nothing; there is a clear difference between flicking someone on the forehead and not doing so. But there is no comparably clear difference between donating all your belongings to charity, and keeping a penny. There is simply no notable difference separating the person doing their best from the one doing their second-best.

III.

As a general rule of thumb in life, it is always helpful to look at what the true theory says for inspiration. This case is no different, and since scalar utilitarianism tells us to stop evaluating things simply as right or wrong, preferring better than and worse than, I think we had better be inspired.

Even if we don’t want to embrace the truth, there is an important insight here: Facts about better or worse1 are the ground truth, and right and wrong are partitions of this. At every moment you have a long list of actions (at least epistemically). Each of them will result in different things happening, different rights being respected or broken, and so on—that is, all of them lie on a scale of greater and lesser rightness/wrongness. When we call some things “forbidden,” “permissible,” “obligatory,” and “supererogatory,” we are drawing lines across this spectrum.2

There may be some natural places to draw some of the lines. For instance, a strict deontologist might think that all actions that involve doing harm lie below all actions that do not, and so we can safely draw a line there. Similarly, we might draw a line at the level of rightness that being dead and doing nothing has.

In fact, even if you don’t accept this as a general representation of rightness, all I need is that it is right for representing beneficence—and this is hard to deny. A spectrum may be hard to accept in certain cases, but once you clear the bar of not doing anything actively bad, it is clear that positive good-doing lies on a spectrum. Whatever good thing you do, you could always do slightly better or slightly worse.

IV.

What the beast inside us covets is to find the place on the scale that divides the merely permissible from the supererogatory. Considering the above representation, the prospects of success look grim. It is not good enough to just do nothing, but on the path between doing nothing and doing perfect is a continuous spectrum of doing progressively better.

Drawing a line demarcating what is “good enough” is a fool’s errand, as anyone who’s thought about vagueness should agree. And since the duty of beneficence (in some cases) has to be satisfied in order for your actions to be right, the idea that there are simply some right actions and some wrong actions—and that you should do the right ones and not do the wrong ones—is untenable. At all times you have a continuum of options available to you, some better than others. There is no line you can draw below which things start being wrong, and there is no line above which everything is supererogatory icing on the cake.

In fact, even if there were a line to be found somewhere in platonic heaven, we certainly do not have enough evidence to determine where it is. Hence you may act above the line, but you would never be able to know, and so the beast inside you must go to bed hungry.

Instead of concerning ourselves with finding the dividing lines, we should instead just look to the base facts which our categories are divisions of: The spectrum of greater and lesser rightness. We can’t ever say that you did enough—any talk of living up to your duty of beneficence dissolves into imperfect talk of degrees of rightness. All we can ever truly say is: more better good.

V.

It’s easy to underestimate how radical this conclusion is, until you have internalized it for some time. There is never anything that is good enough. Not because you always fall short of some threshold, but because there is no threshold to fall short of to begin with. All you have is more reason to do better, but no reason to stop anywhere in particular.

You are left to your own devices, to decide how good you want to be, and where you want to stop. No one can fault you for having stopped where you did, and at the same time you are always at fault for not having gone a little further. It is completely your own responsibility to decide how far you go, and no amount of theorizing can give you an answer, because the question of where to stop is empty.

This is an uncomfortable truth that I’m constantly reminded of in my life. I always hope that I get to a point where I can dust off my hands, and have done what I need to. But the scandal of ethics is that you have to decide for yourself. You can simply do better or do worse, but no one can ever tell you where on the scale is good enough, as there is no such place—the only equilibrium is at the very top where no one ever reaches.

VI.

There is a crutch available: To decide on arbitrary principles to follow. It is not psychologically sustainable to constantly be evaluating and reevaluating the level of your beneficence. So at some point you simply have to decide on a baseline for yourself. If you are like me, doing this makes everything inside you hurt from the sheer arbitrariness of it all. Alas, this feeling is inescapable unless you are perfect—and thus inescapable.

Going into this post, I only intended it as an argument in normative ethics. But through what I can only assume to be divine providence, my reflections have naturally led me to a place where I can shoehorn in Effective Altruist propaganda.

As said, an excellent way of combatting the despair that follows the realization that beneficence knows no limits, is to settle on some arbitrary amount of good to do. With the Giving What We Can Pledge, this decision is made for you. If you take the pledge, you pledge to give away 10% of the money you earn throughout your life to charity.

For most people able to read this, giving away 10% of your income will not negatively affect your life very much. At the same time it will be able to positively affect the lives of a huge number of beings—be they humans, non-human animals, or both. And most importantly, it gives you a baseline to lean on, alleviating the massive burden of having to decide how much good to do.

Is 10% arbitrary? Yes. But so is any amount. Is 10% enough? There is no answer to this question. What we can say is that 10% of your income is quite a bit more than the average person, and enough to make sure that the world would have been a worse place without you. It would be better to decide to give more, and you can always decide to give extra on top of this, but it is a nice round number to have as a baseline.

Taking the pledge carries no legal obligations—it is simply a sincere public statement that you intend to do what it says. And having taken it (or even without taking it), it is very easy to set up recurring donations to various charities, in order to reach the goal. So you never have to expend effort, and you can rest at ease, knowing that you are doing something.

Take The Pledge

I myself took the pledge not long ago. And to anyone following in my footsteps, taking the pledge in response to this post, I will gift a lifetime paid subscription to Wonder and Aporia as an extra carrot.3

Next-best after taking the pledge is subscribing and sharing.

Subscribe now

1

Better and worse may sound too consequentialist for some. It’s easy to talk this way for a consequentialist as facts about rightness don’t come apart from facts about goodness, but I should strictly speak about “more and less right” to keep it theory-neutral.

2

I here represent “obligatory” the way I do, as the spectrum is an evaluation of concrete actions available to you. Obligation is not plausibly a property of specific actions, but of sets of actions. For instance, it may be obligatory that you save a life in some situation, but there is no particular way of doing so that is obligatory (you may both save the drowning child by wading into the pond, or by swimming), what is obligatory is that you take one of the actions.

Particular actions may be permissible, or supererogatory, or forbidden, but the only case in which a single action is obligatory is when all other actions available to you are forbidden.

3

And as a stick, I’ll be very sad if you don’t.

item.title: The Golden Rule Is True
item.content:encoded:
Do unto others as you would have them do to you.
Luke 6:31

Thus speaketh the LORD, and thus speak many other smart people in various cultures around the world. The golden rule seems to have some sort of sticking power, being perhaps the most widespread moral principle ever. But is it true? Aye say I!

Interpretational Gymnastics

To evaluate its truth, though, we have to get clear on what it even means. It may seem straightforward, but the “as you would have them do to you”-part can be interpreted in many different ways, some of which are straightforwardly false.

I.

For instance, we might read the rule as being about what you would actually like de re—that is, prescribing the things you really like. That would be absurd though! To steal an example from fellow blog-haver and golden rule-critic :

You really like hummus, and would love to be sprayed with it every day. Treating others as you’d want to be treated yourself, you load up your hummus cannon and start firing.

I don’t think you’ll be invited back for dinner ever again, yikes—so that can hardly be the right reading.

II.

What if we instead read the principle de dicto? That is, it tells you to do to others “as you would have them do to you—whatever that turns out to be.” Clearly a better reading! But solve one problem, and more just rear their ugly heads.

In “as you would have them do to you” there is a “would” which indicates that we’re in the subjunctive mood. In other words, we have to get modal. To evaluate what you would have someone do to you, when we read this de dicto, we have to know which circumstance we’re considering to know what you would like to have done to you in that circumstance.

Putting it another way, we’re evaluating a counterfactual situation where you’re in the place of the person you’re considering acting towards—and depending on how we specify that situation, your desires might differ, changing the prescription of that goldenest of rules.

One way would be to imagine transporting yourself as you actually are into the position of the person. With this we inherit most of the problems from the de re reading though: Doing it this way, the preferences in question are those that you actually have, and so we are again spraying hummus all over the place.

A better suggestion is to imagine that we pick up your metaphysical essence and put it into a qualitative duplicate of the person you’re evaluating.1 In that case you inherit the preferences of the person you’re considering, meaning the principle really becomes “do unto others what they would have you do to them.”2 So really it tells you to fulfill others’ preferences.

III.

As our game of interpretive whack-a-mole nears its end, we are—for completeness’ sake—left with the question of what parts of their preferences to act on. We might crudely divide our preferences into revealed preferences and terminal values.3 Revealed preferences are the things you actually act on, like your preference to scroll Instagram reels for hours instead of doing your mandatory Wonder and Aporia reading (shame!). Terminal values are the things you ultimately care about in themselves—the stuff you live your life to promote, achieve, etc.

On one reading, the golden rule could tell you to act in accordance with the revealed preferences of others. That’s not plausible though; we generally shouldn’t be helping heroin addicts get their next fix asap. Rather we should read it as prescribing that you act in accordance with other people’s terminal values.

But Is It True?

And by the grace of God, we have ended up with a principle that tells you to act in accordance with other people’s welfare, where welfare is understood as preference satisfaction. This is a lucky result, as preference satisfactionism is correct. So not only is this view the correct result of philosophical reasoning, but it has divine vindication!

I.

Or well, the golden rule is not a theory of welfare, but rather a principle for action. One way of getting the principle for action, though—and one that seems very natural—is to make two claims:

  1. You should act in accordance with other people’s welfare.

  2. Welfare consists in the satisfaction of terminal values.

It is plausible to read “as you would have them do to you” as a description of welfare, in which case the golden rule (making the interpretive moves we’ve made here) would state something like these two theses.

So the rule is wrong if there are cases where either of these two claims is wrong—and otherwise correct.

II.

It might seem that there are clear problems with (1). If you think that there are objective goods—i.e. goods that are just good in themselves, and not good for anyone—which are worth promoting, then (1) is wrong. For instance, it would plausibly be wrong to blow up the Taj Mahal, and erect a giant Paul McCarthy Buttplug Gnome in its place, even if no one cared or were harmed. Reason being that there is just something inherently good about beauty.

I’m personally not very partial to these kinds of objective goods. But that needn’t matter, as we can continue our interpretive escapades: As stated,

Do unto others as you would have them do to you,

the golden rule can be read as implicitly restricting its scope to our other-regarding concerns. Specifically, in saying “do unto others” we can read it as saying “insofar as you are acting towards other people, you should…”—it is a principle about interpersonal action, not our duties in general.

Within a Christian context, this reading can be corroborated: The core of Christian ethics is the double commandment of love.

‘Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind.’ [… And] ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’

Matthew 22:37-39

This is the basic stance. The golden rule then provides a principle for acting on the second part—the love for your neighbor. But this doesn’t necessarily exhaust our duties. After all, we might still have duties towards God, which are not captured in the golden rule.

Anyways the point is not to get bogged down in Christian theology. Rather it is that there is clear precedent for reading the golden rule as a rule concerning your other-regarding reasons; it may yet be compatible with additional duties based on objective goods. With this restriction of scope in mind, claim (1) becomes hard to deny!

III.

The question remaining is thus whether (2) is correct—i.e. whether preference satisfactionism is true. Being a copout, my answer is: “That is beyond the scope of this paper.” It’d be a large digression, so I would point you elsewhere if you want to realize the truth.

More interesting for us is whether you need to read the golden rule as preference satisfactionist. It’s certainly a straightforward interpretation. Still, we can bastardize the principle a little to make it compatible with objective list or hedonist views.

Specifically, we can gerrymander the restrictions on the counterfactual scenarios we evaluate. I gave the two options of putting yourself as you are in the other’s place, and transporting your essence into a qualitative duplicate of the other. But what if we instead move your essence into an ideal counterpart of the person you’re considering. So instead of doing what “you would have them do,” you do what “you should want to have them do.”

With this tweak, the gates are open to shoehorn in any extra assumptions you’d like. Maybe any idealized counterpart has preferences that promote objective goods, such as wanting meaningful relationships or to pursue beauty; or maybe any idealized counterpart has preferences that lend themselves to promoting their pleasure.

In this way the golden rule could be made compatible with any theory of welfare: When it asks you to do to others as you would have them do to you, it is really asking you to do as you should ideally have them do to you if you were in their place.

Unlike the other maneuvers I’ve made, this could hardly be taken as a good faith reading of the golden rule. Maybe if you squint your eyes and take a few steps back, you could get there, but it’s not what an inquirer sporting an open mind and heart would land on.

It’s best considered a cheap marketing trick for objective list theorists and hedonists to pander to their Christian audiences claiming “yeah I actually technically accept the golden rule as true [fingers crossed behind the back]”—meanwhile preference satisfactionists are the ones fighting the good fight. What I’m trying to say is that the golden rule really does seem to weakly commit you to something in the direction of preference satisfactionism.

Conflicts of Interest

Just as you thought you could dust off your hands, having finally understood the golden rule and ascertained its truth, I must sadly inform you that there is still a bump in the rug left to flatten. But I promise it’s the last one!

Throughout I have deliberately spoken of “acting in accordance with other people’s welfare.” I chose this helpfully ambiguous phrase because the golden rule doesn’t clearly tell us what to do when making tradeoffs between people’s welfare. When there is only one person you’re considering, you should simply do what is in their interest. But when there are several people, and doing what’s in the interest of one comes at the cost of sacrificing the interests of others, the rule is underdetermined.

—staying true to the name—has argued that the correct interpretation is one that leads to utilitarianism:

If we accept other regarding welfarism and the updated golden rule, then you treat your welfare as equal to others — for you treat them as you’d want to be treated. This means you maximize overall welfare. However, this is the statement of utilitarianism.

I think that’s too quick, as treating others as you would want to be treated underdetermines how to resolve conflicts.4

Suppose Bob is an extraordinarily thick-boned man standing on a footbridge, beneath which Alice and Connor are tied to the tracks, and towards whom a trolley is hurtling… yadayadayada… you can push Bob, killing him, or refrain and let Alice and Connor die.

Let’s say that you push Bob. Have you done to him as you would have him do to you? I hope not! At the same you have in some sense done to Alice and Connor what you would have them do to you. If you refrain from pushing, you will have done to Bob as you would have him do to you, but not done to Alice and Connor as you would have them do to you.

Either way you will have both followed and not followed the golden rule in different respects. The rule simply doesn’t give us enough information to handle this.

Now, one way of collapsing the ambiguity would be to add a clause like “and in case you can’t do that to everyone, maximize the amount you do to others as you would have them do to you.” But another way might be to say “do only unto others as you would have them do to you”—so in cases of conflict, you should refrain from actively doing harm to someone.

Both of these (and more) are ways of resolving conflicts, but the rule itself is too underspecified to tell us which is correct. The golden rule is correct regardless of which we choose, but it doesn’t tell us which to choose. So in his infinite wisdom, God has left more interpretive work left to be done on the golden rule—a sure sign that He wishes moral philosophers to remain employed for millennia to come.

Why the Golden Rule?

Seeing as the golden rule has required so much interpretive work, one might begin to wonder what the point of it really is. Why not just state the properly interpreted rule: “Do unto others as they would actually have you do to them”—perhaps along with some principle for disambiguating conflicts.

The answer, of course, is that its function is not primarily to be a true proposition, but to be a useful meme. It’s supposed to be a practicable maxim, and this it does better than any careful explication. There are especially two features that I see as important in this regard:

  1. It asks you to identify yourself with the person you’re acting towards, rather than simply commanding you to do what is in the other person’s interest. Saying that you should do what is in the interest of the other, and saying that you should do what you would like if you were the other person are perhaps equivalent principles in content—but not in effect.
    Specifically, the golden rule helps with a little thing called “empathy” (heard of it?). By putting yourself in another person’s place, you not only figure out what to do, but you understand why you should do so; namely because doing otherwise would be as bad for them as it would be bad for you if you acted likewise.

  2. The formulation of the golden rule—when combined with a bit of common sense—also seems to lend itself more to promoting terminal values than explicit formulations. If you simply take an outside perspective on another person, you might have a hard time figuring out what is really in their interest, and what just appears to be in their interest. But by imagining yourself being them, it becomes a lot clearer.

I have argued that the golden rule is true, and I stand by that. Nevertheless, its main function is not to be true, but to gesture people in the correct direction. For this reason I don’t think Christians or Confucians5 are doctrinally committed to desire satisfactionism as a theory of welfare—as much as it pains me to admit.

If I were you, I would subscribe to Wonder and Aporia and restack this post, as it would make both of us happy, and help grow the blog.

Share

You Might Also Like:

1

Don’t worry if you think that this describes something impossible. It doesn’t actually have to be you. Instead, we can evaluate the sentence “what I would like to have done to me” in a possible world centered on the person you’re considering, having the indexical “I” pick out that person. That gives the same result and doesn’t require strange metaphysical commitments.

2

There are of course possible middle-positions between these two extremes, but they seem sort of unmotivated, so I take the essence-swap extreme to be most plausible.

3

As always, I have to shout out ’s post with some very good reflections on this topic in relation with preference-satisfactionism.

4

To be fair, the post in question is like 4 years old.

5

I also don’t think the golden rule plays as central a role as a positive principle for ethics as it does in Christianity. (Besides, it is formulated negatively in Confucianism: Do not impose on others what you yourself do not desire.)

item.title: Don't Be Anti-Trans Because of Language
item.description: It doesn't matter whether trans women are women
item.content:encoded:
You’ll be hard-pressed to find a word which has had its definition more thoroughly debated than “woman.” Documentaries, debates, and—yes—even Substack posts have been dedicated to this intractable issue.

But what even is its significance? People often seem to assume that a lot of normative conclusions hinge on whether trans-women fall under the correct definition of “woman,” such as whether we should refer to them as women, whether they may participate in women’s sports, and perhaps even whether we should allow gender-affirming care for minors.

Yet it’s far from obvious why this should be the case. In fact I think it is not the case, and that the question of the meaning of “woman” is an utterly unimportant question. Essentially nothing of any normative interest hinges on how we answer it.

The Knights of Ni

Before I argue for my thesis, let’s consider a short story:

You live in a magical world—a world of knights, enchanters, and British documentary film-makers—and are pursuing your quest for the Holy Grail. In the course of your adventure, you come upon a group of knights with a most wondrous power. They are keepers of sacred words, a hallowed vocation which comes with quite the perk: They can use the sacred words, and their abilities, as they please.

One word in particular is of incomparable power. Its mere mention is enough to strike holy fear into the unfortunate listener, momentarily reducing their existence to pain. I advise only the foolhardy to read on, as I shall now present the word in its raw glory. I can only pray that mediation through the written word and quotation reduces the potency compared to the spoken form. The word is: “Ni.”

The ruthless knights command you to bring them a shrubbery, lest they unleash their sacred words upon your eardrums. Needless to say, your only choice is to comply. In your search you find an old crone in the midst of beating a cat—important work. Desperate for clues you ask her for a lead, but she refuses to comply. You did not think you would ever stoop this low, but seeing no other choice, you say it: “Ni.”

She writhes in horror.

Moral of the Story

Some of you may find this story oddly familiar. I assure you that this feeling is only coincidental.

In any case, disputes over copyrights are not the point right now. The point is, rather, what we can learn from the story. Can it be morally wrong to use certain words in certain cases? The story seems to present a compelling case.

In it, saying “ni” at the old lady will apparently cause her some harm. Given this, it stands to reason that you shouldn't say “Ni” at her. In fact, it seems that it would be morally wrong to do so.

Of course, right now this story isn’t particularly analogous to the topic at hand. Crucially “Ni” isn't a word in the English language, and so avoiding saying it wouldn't be too hard. On top of this, one might think that the harmful effects of “Ni” are greater than those of misgendering. I don’t know to what extent this is right. From what I can tell, misgendering can be somewhat harmful.1

With the power of thought experiments, we can adjust for these flaws; change it so that “Ni” is in common usage, and adjust the harm to the level you deem appropriate—e.g. a well-placed insult about something the receiver is already very insecure about. So:

You live in a magical world and so on and so forth. The language of the land is “Schmenglish”—a language very much like English, except that one of the 2nd person singular pronouns (the one used for old crones) is “Ni.” However, there is a small group of cat-beating crones of particularly ripe age for whom hearing this word directed at them causes quite a bit of distress.

You now stand before the self-same lady, considering whether to say “Ni” to her, or whether to use the less offensive “Neee-Wom,” which—while technically incorrect—would spare her feelings. Still it seems obvious that you shouldn’t say “Ni!” It’ll harm her feelings, and the weight of the case in favor is that it’d be against the conventions of the language (as well as a little more cognitively demanding, I suppose).

This case illustrates how easily considerations based on correct use of language are overturned.

I swear I’ll say the N-word if you don’t subscribe!

Linguistic Reasons or not?

Let’s now zoom out and consider two possible positions the foil of this article—i.e. someone who thinks the correct definition of “woman” matters—might have: That there are no sui generis linguistic reasons, or that there are.

No Linguistic Reasons

First, let’s say you think words mean things, but you don’t think there are sui generis linguistic reasons. That means that whatever reasons the meaning of a word being X give you to use the word to mean X must be provided by the conditions that are sufficient for the word meaning X, and not from the fact of its meaning X. Sorry, that’s very convoluted! Put another way: The justification has to come from the things that determine word meaning, and not from the word meaning itself.

When the crone asks you what drove you to use “Ni” to refer to her, you might offer the justification “well, that’s what ‘Ni’ means.” To test whether this is a good justification on this view, we can substitute in the conditions that determine meaning. Usually this will be something like commons usage (though you can try with whatever theory you prefer), so we get: “ well, that’s how people generally use the word ‘Ni’.”

As an excuse for why you accidentally said what you did, that might be fine, but as a moral justification not so much. How does the fact that other people in other circumstances use a word in a certain way bear on whether what you did here was justifiable? If I slap you in the face, saying “that’s what people usually do” is not much in the way of justification.

Common usage is of course always a good starting point, as it helps with coordination and whatnot. But it’s only a starting point, and when common usage turns out to be harmful, we should generally try to change it.

Linguistic Reasons

So what if you instead think that there are sui generis linguistic reasons? That is, the fact that a word is commonly used a certain way is one thing, but the fact that this makes the word mean that thing is another. And this latter fact of meaning provides additional reason to use the word in that way, over and above the reasons given by the fact of common usage.

Supposing there are these sorts of reasons, they’d surely have to be very weak. While it may be annoying when someone says “that really effects me,” this is hardly any grave moral wrong. Between Bob who tells Alice to “fuck off,” and Alice who tells Bob that she “could care less what you think,” it seems pretty clear that Bob is the worse offender here.

I mean, that’s what the Ni-case showed us to begin with! In it, we made no stipulations as to whether there are linguistic reasons, and it turned out wrong to say “Ni.” So if there are any such reasons, they must be weak enough to not be relevant in this case.

And even if linguistic reasons are quite strong, it might be worth it to ignore them for a while, and change our usage until the common usage changes and the linguistic reasons line up with our other reasons.

Beyond Pronouns

So far I’ve only really been discussing pronoun use and the like. This should be the strongest case for the person who thinks that it matters whether trans women are women according to the correct definition, since it has to do with language use. And even here, we saw that it fails to be of any real importance.

But language use isn’t the only case where this question is taken to matter. If all it was about were pronouns, the attention the question has gotten wouldn’t make much sense. You’ll often see people use “trans women are not real women” or somesuch as a cognitive shortcut to justify any anti-trans position. Be it trans women in women’s sports, gendered bathrooms, or hormone blockers, there’ll invariably be some person somewhere who thinks they can close the issue by saying “um, they’re actually men.”

While saying “trans women are not women” may sound like a substantive statement about the world, appearances can fool; it’s really not. The problem is that no one is disputing the “ground facts” here—or at least, that’s not essential to the disagreement. A pro-trans person and an anti-trans one can (and probably often do) agree on all the facts about biology, hormones, gametes, and whatnot. So when they disagree, they’re disagreeing about how to conceptually carve up these facts.

But how you choose to describe a situation generally has little to no effect on the moral facts around it. When we’re discussing gendered bathrooms, what matters is not facts about meaning, but facts about safety, rapes, perceived insecurity, or whatever. It’s true that the object of the dispute might center on something resembling a meaning question—namely how broadly to use the “women” in “women’s bathrooms”—but the relevant factors for deciding the issue are not meaning facts.

Similarly, what’s relevant in the question of puberty blockers are facts about health effects, informed consent, and rates of regret; not whether the statement “trans women are women” comes out true on the best theory of meaning.

There are of course often factual disagreements that are heavily correlated with answers to the meaning question. For instance, I suspect that people who think that the biological criterion of womanhood is correct are much more likely to think that misgendering is not a big harm, compared to those who think a social criterion is correct.

My point is not to decide these issues here. In fact, it’s probably a case-by-case thing, and it would be naive to think that a single definition of “woman” will be optimal in all cases in question. My point is simply that the question of the actual meaning of “woman” is completely frivolous—what matters are the first-order facts.

Please identify as a Wonder and Aporia subscriber.

Share

1

Based on a cursory search. E.g. this study on misgendering (which found a small but significant correlation between misgendering and anxiety, though not between misgendering and depression/well-being); and this systematic review of transphobia more generally (which found correlations with negative health outcomes).

item.title: What Is Question-Begging?
item.content:encoded:
Be it Reviewer #2 or some random reply-guy, the neural pathway between reading an argument and saying the words “question-begging” is very short and well-trained among those learned in the ways of philosophy. As soon as there is an argument people disagree with, it seems someone will inevitably deem it question-begging.

In spite of this, figuring out what it means to beg the question is quite a hairy issue once you consider it more thoroughly. The textbook definition is something like: An argument begs the question when the premises assume the truth of the conclusion. That might sound neat, but it’s very hard to make work. To remain justified in rapid-firing on the question-begging accusations, we ought to try to find an answer here. Anything else would be question-begging.

Not a Formal Feature

As said, it’s tempting to give an account where begging the question is a matter of the premises assuming the truth of the conclusion. More specifically, it has to be the conjunction of the premises that has to assume the truth of the conclusion. After all, we can have question-begging arguments like:

  1. The Bible says that God exists

  2. Everything The Bible says is true

  3. Therefore God exists

Neither (1) nor (2) require that (3) is true on their own. Instead the problem is that the two premises in conjunction require the truth of the conclusion. So that’s the answer: An argument begs the question just in case the truth of the premises assume the truth of the conclusion.

Whoopsie! That’s probably not a good definition, as it makes every deductively valid argument question-begging. Consider the textbook argument:

  1. All men are mortal

  2. Socrates is a man

  3. So Socrates is mortal

The claim that all men are mortal, and that Socrates is a man certainly assume that Socrates is mortal. If Socrates were not mortal, then that would provide a counterexample to at least one of the premises, so they must assume that he is.

The problem should be pretty obvious: The standard definition of validity is that the premises jointly entail the truth of the conclusion—the premises could not be true without the conclusion also being true. But if the premises cannot be true unless the conclusion is true, then they certainly assume the truth of the conclusion!

[For a more thorough discussion of this point, and some other relevant issues, I recommend ’s excellent post on the subject. I also just recommend their blog on the whole!]

Not Inherent to Arguments

Begging the question isn’t about the truth-conditions of the premises and conclusions in the argument, or the relations between these. That is, it’s not inherent to the argument itself.

Rather, begging the question is about the epistemic features of the argument in relation to some dialectical context. In actual usage, arguments are not just arguments for a particular proposition, but arguments against alternatives (where an alternative to P is just a proposition that entails ¬P). Suppose I give the argument:

  1. I turned off the stove when I left

  2. If I turned off the stove when I left, then it’s still off

  3. So the stove is still off

If the context here is that we are out for dinner, and you ask whether the stove is off, this seems like a perfectly appropriate argument, even if explicitly saying (2) may be a little odd.

However, if the context is instead that our arsonist neighbor has been sneaking into our house when we’re away and turning on the stove, then it suddenly seems question-begging! Nothing about the argument itself changed. The problem instead lies in the change of targets.

In the first argument, the target alternative to the conclusion is something like that I forgot to turn off the stove. By giving the argument I express that I have a clear and distinct memory of turning off the stove, and this is sufficient to disprove the alternatives we consider relevant in the “dialectical” context.

In the second case, one of the relevant alternatives is our neighbor having turned on the stove. My giving the argument is not much help here, as you obviously won’t accept (2) given the alternative in question. In the first case our neighbor turning on the stove is strictly speaking still an alternative, but it’s so far out and unlikely that it doesn’t matter whether the argument works against it.

Is the correct account then just that question-begging arguments fail to rule out relevant alternatives? It can’t quite be that. The argument above really does strictly rule out the arsonist neighbor-alternative. What makes it problematic or question-begging is that you would never accept (2) unless you already thought that the alternative in question had been ruled out.

Instead we have to zoom out one step, and look at the justifications for the premises, rather than the premises themselves. More specifically, arguments only beg the question with regards to some person (usually your interlocutor), and with regards to some alternative. They do this when the premises presuppose the falsity of the alternative in question in order to have any force.

Or put in analytic philosophese:

An argument begs the question against an alternative A for some agent S, just in case the reasons S has for believing1 the premises presuppose the falsity of A.2

The obvious next question is then what in the world “presuppose” is supposed to mean, as that word is doing a lot of the heavy lifting. I'll give an example to explain it, before I give the definition.

You come home and see what appears to be an apple on your table. Having studied some early analytic philosophy, you reason:

  1. Here is an apple

  2. Therefore there is at least one apple on my table

If we’re a little charitable, we can allow that this is a valid argument. Not only that, but it seems to be of a non-question-begging kind!

However, now you remember that you actually have a lot of fake plastic apples lying around after you decided to order 1000 online because you wanted 1000 plastic apples. You wonder whether the thing on your table is an apple or a replica. To clear yourself of doubts, you reason:

  1. Here is an apple

  2. Therefore there is at least one apple on my table

First, it should be clear that the argument is fine in the first instance, and question-begging in the second. That’s because in the first instance, there are no relative alternatives that involve you having appearances as of seeing an apple, whereas there are in the second—and you’re trying to reason against one such alternative.

That is, in the first case, the alternative(s) is something like “there are no apples or apple-like objects on my table”. If this were true (and assuming more elaborate skeptical scenarios are not relevant alternatives either), you would not have the appearance as of seeing an apple. And since your reason for believing in premise (1) is that you have the appearance as of there being an apple on the table, everything checks out.

Your reasons for believing in premise (1) are the same in the second case. However, here the alternative is “there is a plastic apple on my table”. If this alternative were true, you’d still have the appearance as of there being an apple there, and so it doesn’t work anymore.

Another way of putting the problem in the second case is that for your reasons for believing (1) presuppose that the relevant alternative is true in order for them to justify (1); the reasons you have for believing in (1) can’t make you anymore confident than you already are in the alternative being false.

Again, allow me to translate into philosophese:

An inference from premises P to conclusion C presupposes the falsity of alternative A just in case the reasons for believing P are undercut by A’s being true.

Admittedly, the “undercut” here is still somewhat vague. But this vagueness is sort of deliberate: One way of cashing out the principle is in terms of evidential sensitivity—that the reasons do not reliably distinguish A from P. But I’m not confident that this is the only way arguments can be circular. I think the structure of this account is right, but I’ll leave it open how many ways this “undercutting” can be cashed out.

But yeah, sensitivity is one way, and it’s the one that’s been working in the cases so far. In the apple-case, your visual appearances are not sensitive to the difference between the apple being real and it being plastic; and in the stove-example, your memory can’t tell you whether the arsonist neighbor snuck into your house after you left.

[If you’re interested, I try to flesh out this idea a little more rigorously in this post, in order to show why Moore’s proof of the external world is circular.]

Conclusion

So begging the question is not a feature of arguments themselves. Rather arguments only beg the question against certain alternatives, given certain reasons for believing their premises.

So why do certain arguments feel inherently question-begging? Consider again the argument from the beginning:

  1. The Bible says that God exists

  2. Everything The Bible says is true

  3. Therefore God exists

The reason that arguments like this seem inherently question-begging is that there is no plausible dialectical position where it would ever be convincing to anyone. No one who accepts that everything The Bible says is true would not already believe in God!

But if we imagine some weird Christian who accepted that The Bible is infallible, but were somehow still an atheist, then the argument in question would be perfectly appropriate! They could plausibly be convinced that, “oh yeah, God really does exist!”

Interestingly, the account I give doesn’t obviously capture cases where the problem seems to be purely formal—e.g. where one of the premises just is the conclusion. For instance:

  1. You should subscribe

  2. Therefore you should subscribe

I’m not sure this is a problem, though. It really does seem like this is a different phenomenon than the more interesting cases of begging the question. But if we want, we could just add a clause to the account saying “oh yeah, and also don’t just lump in the conclusion explicitly among the premises”.

You heard it: It’s not question-begging!

Minor Polemical Postscript

At the end of their aforementioned post, Yakiimo claims that this result—that begging the question depends on agents and contexts and whatnot—means that the truths of logic are relativistic in a sense, and that this is very surprising. I think that claim might be a little overblown!

What we’ve shown is that what counts as a good argument is relative. But then I don’t think the truths of logic are about what counts as a good argument. Rather they’re about what inferences preserve truth (at least that’s the sense of logic that would be surprising if it were relative) and that part certainly hasn’t been shown to be relative!
