1

Maybe it should just read “the reasons S has or would give for the premises” or somesuch. After all, arguments can be question-begging even if no one believes them. It just requires that we imagine some reasons that could be given in favor of the premises.

2

This is quite similar to Sinnott-Armstrong’s account that Yakiimo discusses, and it could probably count as a “subjective epistemic account” according the the nomenclature they lay out there.

item.title: Should Politics Affect Science?
item.content:encoded:
The scientist is guided by the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth; or something like that. In their relentless pursuit of the big T (as those in the biz like to call it), the scientist cannot be distracted by such fluffy things as “feelings,” or “morality.”

There are of course ethics committees that make sure that things don’t go completely south. But they act more as deontic side constraints on research than anything. Once a topic has been chosen and a project has been greenlit, the scientist resumes their thankless task of pursuing truth, preconceptions and warm feelings be damned; the scientist should simply attempt to tell the rest of us what is true, and then we can decide what to do with the newfound knowledge.

While perhaps slightly exaggerated, the Platonic ideal of a scientist—or researcher more generally—is not far from this undeterred seeker of truth. Having read this characterization (as well as the title of this post), you can probably guess where I want to go next: Should scientists be unconcerned with value? Or should value guide inquiry?

This post is too long for email. So if you’re reading in email, open it in the app or browser to get the real deal.

The life of a hypothesis

Before answering any question, I have heard that it is often good to know what the question is. Begrudgingly we take this advice, as we make a detour into typical analytic-philosophical pedantry. First, we can separate three stages in the life of a hypothesis:

  1. Inception - The scientist comes up with the hypothesis, and decides to test it out.

  2. Discovery - The scientist does the experiment, tests out the hypothesis, gets some results, and communicates their findings (e.g. with a report published in a journal).

  3. Application - The results are used in the real world. This can be as background/inspiration for other scientists, as a talking point in TikTok live debates, or even to guide policy decisions.

This cute little model helps clarify the question. No one should really question whether values matter in step (3). Obviously they do! Likewise, it is quite plausible that values matter in (1). Both in the sense that ethics committees should make sure that your experiment doesn’t involve, say, killing people,1 and in the sense that we should choose the right things to research. For instance, we should remember to also research women’s health, and not just men’s health.

The real interesting question is whether values should be included in step (2). Specifically in interpretation of results and communication to others. For instance, should we have a higher bar for publishing politically inconvenient results? Should the epistemic standard for significance be higher (e.g. by lower p-values)? Should scientists be biased to interpret ambiguous results in ways that fit with our moral commitments? To these I say yes.

What value?

Our clarificatory adventures are not quite over yet, as there is still an ambiguity in the question. Specifically, we have to get clear on what the “should” here is supposed to stand for. It is possible to mean many different things with “should,” but of particular interest to us here are the epistemic and moral variants.

What should you do epistemically? Something like whatever best lets you get true beliefs. The epistemic saint is unconcerned with anything but the truth—not unlike our scientist from above.

What should you do morally? Oof, I wish I could tell you, but that’s a bit harder! Probably donate some money to charity and not harm others. But that’s not really the important part right now. Instead what’s important is that you should probably morally do and care about things that regard other stuff than acquiring true beliefs.

While it may seem trivial, this thrilling digression allows us to dissolve the question somewhat. We can’t just ask “should values guide inquiry?” Or at least if we do, we can now be explicit with what we mean with the unqualified “should.”

Shouldepistemic we have our (moral/political) values guide inquiry? That hardly makes sense! At least if we think that the truth is out there to discover, independent of how we feel about it. Maybe there can be value in taking our values into account (for instance if a predominance of males in archeology leads to biased interpretations of evidence), but only as instrumental in getting accurate beliefs.

Shouldmoral we have values guide inquiry? Almost certainly! How we shouldmoral conduct our inquiry is in the way that’s morally best (duh)! Maybe doing so ends up looking a lot like acting in accordance with how we shouldepistemic (we’ll get to that), but it’s at least an open question!

So which “should” is the right one? One option is that there is not really an answer here. All there is to say is that you shouldepistemic pursue truth, and shouldmoral maybe do other stuff sometimes—but no one can tell you what you shouldØ do. Scary!

Or perhaps there is a true “should,” which is a sort of plurality of the relative “shoulds,” so that we have to weigh the different considerations up. Or maybe one of the two simply is the True “should.”

There is a lot that could be said here, but I’ll restrict myself to this: Whatever option we choose, it seems very clear that shouldmoral is a lot more important. If waterboarding some cute puppies and sweet grandmothers would allow me to find out whether Humeanism or non-Humeanism about natural laws is correct, I would be very reluctant! It’s not even clear that a simple firm slap to someone’s face could be justified if it meant figuring out whether the analytic/synthetic distinction is real.

All this is to say: Values certainly shouldmoral guide inquiry—and to the extent that there is a single real “should,” values should also guide inquiry simpliciter.

For all X, you shouldX subscribe to Wonder and Aporia:

Impartiality through the backdoor?

Even if we accept that how we conduct ourselves (even our inquiry) should primarily be guided by moral concerns, it’s still unsettled whether that should lead us to the more grotesquely explicit sorts of value-discrimination, as I listed at the start. We may yet not have to consider the political correctness of our scientific conclusions. Here is a (naive) argument that an interlocutor might give for why we ought to remain value-neutral, even if we accept shouldmoral as primary.2

In a (non-shit) decision theory, you plug in two components: A valuation of each outcome, and the probability of each outcome. Take standard expected utility theory, where you assign the value of an action as the probability-weighted sum of the values of possible outcomes:

The better our probability estimates are, the better decisions we make—information is valuable. So if we learn some new piece of information (like that not reading Wonder and Aporia causes cancer), we’d better factor that into our decisions (by reading Wonder and Aporia), lest we shoot ourselves in the feet.

Case closed, over and done! It’s just obvious: If we have some piece of information, we should use it. That is, the stuff that we shouldepistemic is just a natural corollary of what we shouldmoral (excluding waterboarding-cases and the like).

No

In principle, this argument is right. The problem is that humans and societies are not unbiased machines that take in precise credence-values and spit out EV distributions. If we were, we should just try to optimize the amount and accuracy of information available, and factor all that into our decision-making. But there are several reasons why we should sometimes taint our epistemic practices with values.

The Value Gap

First, there is usually a gap between the evidence you have available, and what beliefs you come to based on it. For example, it might be that the archeological evidence is ambiguous on the division of labor and gender roles in prehistoric society. Perhaps we have generally assumed that women are passive caregivers, and men are active hunters and crafters, but perhaps the evidence is not so strong *wink wink*.

Now, there are two different ways of going here. The first is to say that this masculine bias is epistemically problematic, since it means that we are unjustifiably confident in theories that portray men as dominant, meaning we should correct. This is compatible with saying that we shouldn’t have values in science—we should just correct for them.

The other version—what is called the gap argument in the literature—is to say that there genuinely is indeterminacy here. The evidence is simply not enough to say e.g. whether women helped hunting or not. So whatever conclusion you come to, you’ll have to use some other procedure than pure epistemology to decide where to go. And if we have to choose anyways, then it would surely be absurd to take any conclusion other than the one that fits best with our values! So we just choose to go with the theory that labor was divided equally.

Okay, but even if the evidence doesn’t determine the theory, it will point in one direction, right? Unless your credence distribution is perfectly even over theories, you should favor the one with highest probability. Two things to this:

  1. It’s true that if we simply have to express a credence distribution, then we should just express… our actual credence distribution. But sometimes we have to give a more discrete attitude (like say which theory is best). In those cases it might be best to say that the theory that is normatively better is best, even if it’s not most likely.

  2. Oftentimes your credence-distributions might be vague enough to be genuinely indeterminate. Maybe this isn’t too common in The Hard Sciences™ where experiments are done with numbers—but in cases like the one above, the evidence might genuinely be too ambiguous to say that there is one theory that is clearly more likely.

Technical Note: For a perfect bayesian agent with flawless introspection, there would never be any gap between evidence and theory, since any set of evidence determines a single posterior, given your priors. But if you know any perfect bayesian agent, I’d like to have their number!

We can mitigate first-order imperfection by thinking about higher-order uncertainty. But unless we’re perfect agents, such higher-order uncertainty will always remain imperfect (and if it were precise, you could standardly collapse it into a precise first-order distribution). Hence there will always be some ranges for where our credence-distributions lie, and here we should err in the favor of normatively convenient options.

Besides, if there are, say, several scientists working on a report with different priors, then even if they were perfect Bayesians each, there would be indeterminacy about what conclusion to write down in the report.

Inductive risk

Here I’m drawing on another common argument in the literature: Inductive risk. I’m here drawing heavily on Heather Douglas’ Inductive Risk and Values in Science.

Statistical significance

Often you’ll have a threshold for statistical significance—typically a p-value under 0.053—which indicates whether there is a significant correlation between two measured values. If the correlation is deemed statistically significant, that’s taken as a sign that there’s something funny going on there (i.e. there’s probably some sort of connection between the two), and otherwise not.

If you set your p-value higher, you increase the risk of false positives (finding connections where there are none), and if you lower it, you increase the risk of false negatives (missing connections when they’re there). It’s important to note that statistical significance is a binary judgement: Some result is either deemed significant or not, even though the underlying measure (p-value) is continuous. This will be important.

Now consider something like “safe doses” with regards to carcinogenic compounds. Unless you’re living the ANCAP dream, you’ll probably have the government regulate what are permissible levels of potential carcinogens in various products. In pursuit of this, you might imagine that regulators—among other things—look at what dose levels produce “statistically significant results.” (In fact this is what happens in certain cases. For instance the EU decides Acceptable Daily Intake on the basis of NOAEL, which is sensitive to where you set the threshold for statistical significance.)

So when you’re deciding the p-values you count as statistically significant, you’re making a tradeoff between how many false positives and false negatives you want to allow, and so in turn whether you want to avoid overregulating or underregulating. Depending on how harmful the thing you’re studying is, and how bad regulation might be, it might make sense to adjust what you count as statistically significant. That is, your value judgements should affect your epistemic standards. The more harmful a false negative would be, the harsher your standards, and vice versa.

Obviously this point isn’t just about statistical significance. It generalizes to whenever you have to make a decision about how to draw the limits of any concept used to characterize or convey some scientific results. These decisions aren’t innocent, and while clarity and convention is one factor, you should also factor in moral considerations.

Characterizing evidence

But inductive risk doesn’t only occur on the level of analyzing the data. No, no, no, you also have to make decisions about how you characterize the evidence you collect to begin with. Here Douglas gives the example of a study on the carcinogenic effects of dioxins. Rats were given different doses over two years, after which they were autopsied and examined.

The female rat liver slides have been examined in three different studies, and the results are shown in this table:

That is, the same slides were examined at different times, yielding different assessments for the amounts of tumors. (Btw, the 1978 study “has been central to regulators in setting acceptable levels for dioxins in the environment.” (According to Douglas))

The point is, of course, that evaluating evidence is not a straightforward process. There are many borderline cases of whether something is a tumor or not, or which type it is. Deciding how to classify the evidence requires judgement—and judgements that different expert pathologists do not agree on.

Pathologist Rupert might choose to count all borderline cases as tumors, and all tumors on the border between benign and malignant as malignant. Pathologist Denise might instead choose the opposite. If Rupert is the one who classifies the evidence, the study will find stronger effects, and dioxin might be more heavily regulated; and if Denise does it instead, the study finds weaker effects and dioxin is more loosely regulated. Whether you choose to be a Denise or a Rupert should depend on how you value these two things (or more accurately, how valuable they are).

So when deciding how to classify the evidence, scientists have to take into consideration the political values, such as how highly they value public health compared to lack of regulations—how to conduct your study should not be separated from the moral and political significance of the thing studied.

Science is a social thing

A point that has been sort of lurking in the background for this discussion is the fact that science is a social thing. The three stages of a hypothesis (inception, discovery, application) are not carried out by a single individual. Research is conducted by large groups, and results are applied by people who didn’t do the research (such as policymakers). This whole process requires communication between people many steps of the way.

If you could beam your precise credence-distributions or full datasets into the heads of other people, and be sure that they’ll act on these with the right values in mind, then we’d perhaps have no problems. Scientists should then collect data and pass it on losslessly. There are two important differences which make this dream not work:

  1. Sadly, none but the most hardcore rationalists communicate in credence distributions. Instead people use these “words,” such as “statistically significant,” to communicate their results. Scientists write things such as “strong relationship,” “cannot rule out,” and “provides evidence that” in their abstracts and conclusions. These phrases don’t convey the full story, but describe it—and depending on how you describe it, people might get different impressions, even if the data is the same. So depending on the moral and political significance of the topic in question, scientists should adapt how they describe their research.

    More generally, since communication is imperfect, the goal should maybe not always be to communicate results as accurately as possible, but to do so in as morally responsible a way as possible. These two might often coincide, but not always, and when they don’t, scientists shouldmoral plausibly sacrifice epistemic considerations for moral ones.

  2. Even if communication weren’t imperfect, many people have messed up values, or are simply stupid.

    Suppose that scientists found strong evidence that trans people are not “born that way.” This might have relevance for certain issues, but it shouldn’t affect whether people respect and accept trans people more generally. Sadly, it does! For inscrutable reasons, people often take certain questions like these to be normatively relevant, even when they aren’t.

    So while communicating these results would increase understanding, it would also risk adverse moral effects. The point here isn’t that the scientists shouldn’t communicate the results, or communicate them accurately—the case is too abstract to say—but to illustrate that it should at least be a reason that is taken into consideration.

Since science is social, it involves imperfect communication, and communication to imperfect people. This means that scientists should take the effects and interpretations into account, rather than merely their truth-value.

In conclusion: qualifications

Maybe you thought that we were done making distinctions at this point. If so, you probably missed the fact that this is a philosophy post. When it comes to any normative issue, there are three broad levels of application to consider:

  1. Laws

  2. Norms

  3. Individual decisions

For our case these would apply as follows:

  1. Should our laws make science guided by values?

  2. Should we have norms among scientists that their research be guided by values?

  3. Should scientists sometimes (or often) make decisions within their research based on values?

To the first question, my answer is more or less no. There should probably be legal restrictions on the “inception” and “application” stages of a hypothesis (e.g. restrictions on human and animal testing). But I can’t see any plausible reason that the discovery stage should have legal restrictions.

On question (2), the answer is unclear. All the reasons I have given in this post count in favor of a “yes.” Still, anyone experienced in the ways of consequentialism would know that it’s very hard to give clear answers to these things.

I can imagine various adverse effects that could arise from value-guided science becoming normalized—especially if the norms are explicit. People might start to lose trust in science (or certain fields), and decisions be made on worse grounds. Or perhaps certain biases or norms become too ingrained, leading to so extensive inaccuracy that the moral considerations do more harm than good. In any case, notice that the reasons here are still moral/political, rather than epistemic.

I’m pretty sure that the answer to (3) is yes! There are lots of places where science has room for values (such as in the tumor-diagnosing case), and in these, scientists should choose to act on the better values (duh). It is naive to think that science can be neatly separated from everything else; just like any other activity, it involves actions and has effects. Whenever these features crop up, we have to take reasons into consideration—scientists are no exception.

It has been scientifically proven that you should subscribe to Wonder and Aporia and share this post.

item.title: Bleeding Heart Utilitarianism
item.description: Acting immorally for the sake of others
item.content:encoded:
There are many proposed counterexamples to utilitarianism. Take for instance T.M. Scanlon’s Transmitter Room Case from What We Owe to Each Other:

Suppose that Jones has suffered an accident in the transmitter room of a television station. Electrical equipment has fallen on his arm, and we cannot rescue him without turning off the transmitter for fifteen minutes. A World Cup match is in progress, watched by many people, and it will not be over for an hour. Jones’s injury will not get any worse if we wait, but his hand has been mashed and he is receiving extremely painful electrical shocks. Should we rescue him now or wait until the match is over?

Assuming the number of people watching is large enough and invested enough in the game, it would seem a utilitarian is committed to answering: Yes, we’ll let him wait until the match is over.

Or perhaps the consider the sheriff-case from H.J. McCloskey’s An Examination of Restricted Utilitarianism:

Suppose that a sheriff were faced with the choice either of framing a Negro for a rape that had aroused hostility to the Negroes [sic] (a particular Negro [sic!] generally being believed to be guilty but whom the sheriff knows not to be guilty)—and thus preventing serious anti-Negro [SIC!] riots which would probably lead to some loss of life and increased hatred of each other by whites and Negroes [you get the point]—or of hunting for the guilty person and thereby allowing the anti-Negro riots to occur, while doing the best he can to combat them.

Again it seems a utilitarian is committed to framing the Ne person, since doing so will avert more harm than what is done to the person framed.

These verdicts are, uh, unsavory, and make many people think that utilitarianism is false. I definitely see where they’re coming from, and it’s the main thing that keeps me from fully embracing the view. So let’s grant that utilitarianism is false for now.

What now? We may still embrace:

Bleeding Heart Utilitarianism: Whether or not utilitarianism is false, we choose to take on the sin of immorality out of concern for others.

This may sound a little strange, but the fundamental idea is straightforward: Utilitarianism is the only moral theory that only cares about the people’s interests.

Deontologists (and others) might object to this particular way of phrasing it, but the underlying point is undeniable: If you just care about people’s interests and welfare, you’ll be utilitarian.

Take the familiar footbridge variation of the trolley problem. The thick-boned man has an interest in not being pushed over the footbridge and killed. And importantly, he doesn’t have any particular interest in not being pushed by a moral agent—he’d be just as sad if a strong gust of wind blew him onto the tracks.

On the other hand, the five people on the tracks also have interests in not being run over, such that the interests are overall in favor of the fat man ending up on the tracks. If you were looking at the situation from afar, you should hope that a gust of wind blew the guy; and if he were already on the tracks, you definitely shouldn’t save him!

But many theories other than utilitarianism will say that you shouldn’t push him. Bleeding Heart Utilitarianism says: “Maybe that’s true, but we do it anyway, out of concerns for others.” Remember, the guy isn’t hurt anymore by you pushing than by the wind pushing, so if you really care about others, you should allow your hands to get dirty—sacrifice yourself to sin—for the sake of those involved.

Or, take the sheriff case from above. Again, the person doesn’t care whether it’s a moral agent that frames her, or whether people think she’s guilty for other reasons. If incriminating evidence materialized through quantum fluctuations, she’d be no less distressed!

And the reason utilitarianism tells you to frame her is that even worse stuff will happen if you don’t! Maybe people will get lynched, who have at least as strong an interest in not being killed as the innocent person has in not being framed. So if you really care about people, you frame the innocent person, tainting your own moral purity.1

If you were behind a veil of ignorance, not knowing which of the people you were, or if you had to live through the lives of everyone involved, you would want yourself to commit the immoral act. So if you care about others, you’ll do so.

Bleeding Heart Utilitarianism isn’t a moral theory—it’s a lifestyle!2 We don’t say that what we do is moral, but we simply can’t stand to see suffering, so we do what’s best for others, rights and duties be damned! We sacrifice our own moral sainthood for the sake of the things that we really think matter.3

If you care about what’s best, you’ll subscribe and share

Share

1

Maybe you wouldn’t actually hope that evidence materialized, or that a gust of wind blew the guy. In that case, I think you just judge that it’d not be good—e.g. maybe sadistic pleasure isn’t good. But Bleeding Heart Utilitarians (or Bleeding Heart Consequentialists at any rate) can agree with your judgements, or accept the disagreements of axiology. But it can be accommodated within the framework.

2

Of course, explicitly acting on utilitarian principles is not a good idea, and not recommended by utilitarianism. But we still get the result that we just ignore what the “true” theory says for all normative-ethical purposes.

3

I recall having a similar post to this, but I couldn’t find it. In any case, the idea is very much in his vein/inspired by him.

item.title: The Critic's Advantage
item.description: Against tearing down without building up
item.content:encoded:
There are many difficulties with markets. Externalities, public goods, and monopolies all make markets operate in troublesome ways. Absent—arguably quite hefty—interventions, markets fail us. In the face of this fact, many have decided that markets are stupid and evil! So-called “market logic” is probably not even deductively valid, if you ask these people (though logicians are still working on that).

The problem is of course what to replace them with. Despite all their flaws, markets are incredibly good at distributing resources. When this is working as usual, we don’t really notice it, but it becomes a huge headache once you try to find something to replace them with. Alas, this is easy to miss, when you are simply critiquing the option on the table, examining only its flaws.

This is the critic’s advantage: Finding flaws in a proposal or theory is often trivial. However, in many cases every possible option will have flaws. For this reason, the non-committal critic can seemingly show any target to be ludicrous, even if it’s the best option.

This post is not about markets. You can think what you will about markets (personally big fan). The critic’s advantage, however, is ubiquitous once you notice it—especially in philosophy.

Perhaps the best example is population ethics. The repugnant conclusion is… well the name really says it all. For the uninitiated, it is the view that for any population of exceedingly happy people, there is a much larger population whose lives are barely worth living but which is at least as good.

I can’t find any numbers on this, but my sense is that most of those who know about it don’t accept it—and certainly find it, well, repugnant upon first hearing about it. For this reason, people are also not very positively disposed towards the total view in population ethics (according to which the sum total of welfare in a population is all that matters), since the repugnant conclusion straightforwardly follows from this view.

This is the critic’s advantage at play: The repugnance of the repugnant conclusion—together with the fact that the total view implies it—is taken as a clear slam dunk against the view; the total view can simply be dismissed.1

Core to the critic’s advantage, however, is that it is illusory. A theory is not clearly wrong, just because it implies the repugnant conclusion; every theory in population ethics will be problematic, and there are very strong arguments in favor of the conclusion. As argues (drawing of course heavily on Parfit), you can only avoid the repugnant conclusion if you reject one of these other principles:

  1. Benign addition: It is not bad to improve the life of the people who exist, as well as creating more people with worthwhile lives.2

  2. Non-anti-egalitarianism: A more equal distribution of welfare is not worse than a less equal one.3

  3. Transitivity: If x is better than y, and y is better than z, then x is better than z.

If you want to deny the repugnant conclusion, you’ll have to deny at least one of these. So while a theory that vindicates the repugnant conclusion might seem ridiculous on its face, this consideration only has the force it does so long as you refuse to commit to a position yourself. Once you do, comparable grotesquery will follow.

Likewise in decision theory. Anyone can tell you that expected value fanaticism has unsavory implications. God offers the following game to you:

Verily, I say unto thee: I cast a fair coin, even until it falleth upon heads. If heads appeareth upon the first casting, lo, I bestow upon thee two days in My kingdom. If it cometh upon the second casting, thou shalt inherit four days. If upon the third casting, behold, eight days shall be thine. Every tail that precedeth the first head doth double the portion afore given. This is the manner of the game. What sum, therefore, wilt thou render to partake thereof?

A consistent expected value fanatic will pay any amount whatsoever, since the expected value of this game is infinite. They’d endure billions of years of torture, just for a single chance to play this! That’s crazy! For this reason, many dismiss EV fanaticism out of hand.

Again we have come upon the critic’s advantage. So long as you offer no decision theory of your own, this sounds perfectly legitimate. But as points out, any theory that rejects this result must also accept either:

  1. Intransitivity: if A is better than B, and B is better than C, C is sometimes better than A.

  2. Timidity: for some guaranteed payout X, a 99.9999999999999999999% chance of some payout vastly better than X is worse than a guarantee of X.

As well as other nasty results. Anyone can point and laugh, and, when asked what theory they give instead, say “uh, I’m not really sure, but definitely not that.” That will make your position appear sounder than it is, however. The point is not that it’s not okay to be uncertain, but the uncertainty should not be one-sided—it should not turn into a tactical non-committment, which lets you avoid the result you don’t like, without having to deal with the implausibility of what follows.

I could make this article arbitrarily long, but I think that’d start getting boring quickly. The point should be clear enough: Don’t think that the critic’s advantage is genuine.

This pattern crops up again and again, particularly in ethics4—and particularly against more “principled” views. Maybe you can think of one counterintuitive case to utilitarianism, or maybe caring about animal welfare leads you to crazy-sounding places. That’s all well and good. But the minimally reflective people who hold these kinds of views are not unaware of this fact. They have simply noticed that these judgements are results of principles that we had better not reject.

I for one respect the principled system-builders. The people who actually decide to take a theory and run with it, rather than collecting together the judgements that would be nice to have, and hoping that some day, somehow, someone will find a way to make them work.

Not subscribing to Wonder and Aporia commits you to very bad things for complicated reasons you wouldn’t understand.

Share

You Might Also Like:

1

I am not saying that this is the attitude people who actually think seriously about the issue think. But it’s an attitude I get the sense that many people on the internet have.

2

For simplicity, I have formulated this as an action performed on a population. This is strictly speaking wrong, as the repugnant conclusion is about the value of worlds, not the rightness of actions. The formulation from Huemer is:

If worlds x and y are so related that x would be the result of increasing the well-being of everyone in y by some amount and adding some new people with worthwhile lives, then x is better than y with respect to utility.

3

Again this is a simplification. The official statement is:

If x and y have the same population, but x has a higher average utility, a higher total utility, and a more equal distribution of utility than y, then x is better than y with respect to utility.

4

Though not limited to ethics. For instance, I think the free will debate might also be vulnerable to this. It is easy to point out that determinism seems incompatible with free will (with something like the control argument), without considering whether indeterminism might also be incompatible (through something like the luck objection). And vice versa.

item.title: How Bad Is the Idealist's Mantra?
item.description: The only things you see are the only things you see
item.content:encoded:
There is a certain platitude that idealists have repeated again and again since time immemorial. Berkeley says it best:

It is indeed an opinion strangely prevailing amongst men, that houses, mountains, rivers, and in a word all sensible objects, have an existence, natural or real, distinct from their being perceived by the understanding. But, with how great an assurance and acquiescence soever this principle may be entertained in the world, yet whoever shall find in his heart to call it in question may, if I mistake not, perceive it to involve a manifest contradiction. For, what are the fore-mentioned objects but the things we perceive by sense? And what do we perceive besides our own ideas or sensations? And is it not plainly repugnant that any one of these, or any combination of them, should exist unperceived?1

Though old, this mantra is alive and kicking:

I think captures the idea well:

While it might sound plausible at first, it’s just a bad inference, since it conflates epistemology with ontology. The idea is basically:

  1. Experience is more epistemically fundamental than physical objects.

  2. So experience is more ontologically fundamental than physical objects.

The problem is that the general inference:

  1. X is more epistemically fundamental than Y.

  2. So X is more ontologically fundamental than Y.

Is demonstrably wrong!

Suppose that you’re taking a nice walk along the beach, when you come across a trail of footprints. Seeing these, you infer that a person walked here recently. In this case, the footprints are epistemically prior to your knowledge of the person walking. Does it follow that the footprints are ontologically more fundamental than people walking? No!

Or consider other people’s mental states. The way I know that you feel pain when I kick you in the groin (hypothetical)

unless…

is that I see you on the ground, curled up and yelling slurs at me. So your writhing and swearing is epistemically more fundamental for me than your pain. But that doesn’t mean that your behavior is in itself more fundamental than your pain—the pain is what causes your behavior.

So this inference pattern is clearly bunk! In fact, it is usually exactly wrong: We almost always infer the more fundamental things from the less fundamental ones, such that the epistemic and ontological relations run in reverse.

There is also another possible way of reading the point, which is something like:

  1. We only ever contact/know things through experiences.

  2. So experiences are all that exist.

But again, the inference:

  1. We only ever contact/know things through X.

  2. So X is all there is.

Is also clearly wrong! The pain example is a good one: I only ever know of other people’s experiences through their behavior, but it doesn’t follow that their behavior (or my experience of their behavior) is all that exists. Similarly, we only know about bacteria through microscopes (or other macroscopic phenomena), but that doesn’t mean that only microscopes and no bacteria exist.

Berkeley Redux?

While this particular set of inferences is clearly faulty, there might still be a nearby idea that is salvageable.

Specifically, you could imagine that you accept two theses:

  1. A dualist picture makes no sense.

  2. The phenomenal cannot be reduced to the physical.

Perhaps you believe (1) because you cringely accept the interaction problem, or perhaps you think there’s some deeper incoherence. And for (2) you’ve perhaps read some Chalmers, or maybe you have other reasons for thinking this.

It doesn’t really matter why you believe these. The point is that if you believe them, then the mantra from above may in fact carry some weight. The reason is that while epistemic priority doesn’t establish ontological priority, it generally ensures that the epistemically prior thing cannot be shown to not exist by epistemically posterior things.

Or perhaps put more carefully, some evidence cannot be overturned by anything inferred from that evidence.

This might sound overly strong at first, and you’ve surely come up with a counterexample or two as you’re reading this. For instance, by using and investigating solid objects in the world, we’ve discovered that the objects in question are almost entirely empty, and so not, in fact, solid. So the evidence involving solid objects (such as screens) shows that that was not what the evidence was to begin with.

Or for a more mundane example, suppose you see a person with a straw-hat. Later you return to the same place, and see something with that same straw-hat, and see that it’s actually a scarecrow. From the first piece of evidence, you infer that it’s the same thing wearing the hat, but of course that undermines the evidence itself, since it was not in fact a person you saw.

The problem with these counterexamples is that they’re way too inflationary with how they characterize our evidence, conflating our interpretation of the evidence with what the evidence actually is. Our evidence wasn’t that we saw solid objects or people with hats, but what appeared to be solid objects or people with hats. And the later inferences can’t undermine that even if they change our interpretation or the evidential support relations.

Returning to the person who believes that:

  1. A dualist picture makes no sense.

  2. The phenomenal cannot be reduced to the physical.

If they then also accept the first part of the idealist mantra, along the lines of:

  1. (Phenomenal) experiences are epistemically prior(/all there is/all our evidence).

They can infer to idealism from the principle we just considered. After all, if the phenomenal cannot be reduced to the physical, and dualism doesn’t make sense (in the sense that there can’t both be mind and matter existing separately), then it follows that either the phenomenal or the physical is unreal.2 But (3) in combination with the principle that evidence cannot be undermined by its implications, it follows that the physical is unreal, giving us idealism.

Another way of putting the point is that the physical stuff is easy to construct out of experiences. Or rather the appearance of physical stuff is easy to construct, but then the appearance of physical stuff is also all we have for certain.

Now, the cool kids of Substack are of course pulling out hairs right now, yelling at the screen, seeing as they’re all apparently illusionists—and often even cooler-sounding things like meta-illusionists and qualia quietists. The problem is that they won’t accept (3), at least if we include the (phenomenal). We only have the appearance or illusion of phenomenal experience (or maybe not even that for the fancier views), but it’s not some evidential given and can be debunked by other considerations—for instance that these supposed phenomenal experiences don’t fit with a physical ontology.

We do have experiences, but these are something like representational or functional states. These are certainly not irreducible to the physical, and are in fact quite hard to separate from the physical, so nothing really interesting follows here.

But even if we don’t become illusionists or illusionists+, I don’t think that the idealist’s revised argument here goes through either, for the simple reason that (1) is false. At least if we think that we can have a concept of the physical—there’s no contradiction in saying that there is both physical and mental, and that they covary in whatever way. An idealist might disagree that we can have the concept of something physical, but even if that’s right, we can get something that serves the same role with Ramsey sentences. I.e. we don’t commit to any particular properties/relations, but only commit to there being properties/relations that play the role that physical properties/relations should.

I also don’t think that idealists will usually appeal to (1). Rather they’ll appeal to something more modest, like that a dualist picture is redundant, or necessarily less parsimonious than an idealist one.

The problem here is that to the extent that idealism is more parsimonious, it is incredibly strongly disconfirmed by our experience, since our experience consistently is like what one would expect if there were physical objects. So we have very good reason to think that there are physical objects—or at the very least, something playing the structural role of physical objects, which we can (for all intents and purposes) call physical objects.

Nevertheless, the revised version of the argument, while maybe not sound, is at least not obviously fallacious. And for that it deserves credit, I suppose.

Esse est subscripiti
