item.title: Panpsychism For Functionalists
item.content:encoded:
People often hate on panpsychists for the ridiculous view that random physical objects such as rocks are conscious. Haha, very funny! But what if physicalists, including functionalists, are committed to saying the same thing? Not so funny now, is it?

Well, I’ll give an argument here that they are. Not only are they committed to this, but they’re committed to many more random things being conscious than panpsychists are! I can’t promise that this argument is that serious, as it hinges on some fairly specific assumptions; but I can promise that it’s at the very least a fun argument.1

I.

It’s easiest to start with a type-type identity theory. This is the view that mental state types are identical to physical state types. The standard example here (which I’m told people should stop using, but alas here we are) is that Pain = C-fiber firing. That is, the mental state type Pain is identical to the physical state type of C-fiber firing (neuroscientific accuracy notwithstanding).

Now, the type-type identity theory we’ll be considering is one where the physical types are individuated by some fairly large-scale structural properties. For instance some set of properties that is substrate independent. The types might be individuated by some sort of more abstract “graph” network, including the relations between the nodes on the graph—but any microphysical structure (whether carbon-based, silicon-based, cellulose, etc.) that is isomorphic to/satisfies this network, counts as the same type. Perhaps around the level of granularity as this fly brain simulation:

II.

Alright, so now that we’ve defined the theory, take a look at a table in front of you. (Or if you don’t have any, look at this one:

)

Alright, now conceptually abstract away the whole table, leaving you with only a blank canvas of potential table:

You there? Good. Now, at this point, we’ll have to get a little creative, as we’re gonna find ways to represent the various structures that our type-type identity theory looks at, in the form of shapes within the table. For example, we can represent the cell bodies of neurons with spheres, and the axons of neurons with long lines or tubes. What we do now is that we take some type of state that our theory says is conscious, and represent it in the table. For example, suppose that the following structure is conscious according to our theory:

We then add parts of the table back in, in such a way that it satisfies or is isomorphic to this structure:

That is, we focus in on this gerrymandered proper part of the table. Now, if our theory is correct in saying that the type of structure above is identical to some mental state, then the gerrymandered table-piece (let’s call it Tim) that is a token of that type will also be a token of that mental state—so Tim is conscious!

III.

Obviously this is an incredibly oversimplified example! For one, the relevant structures will be a lot more complicated than nodes and edges! But I hope it’s pretty obvious that if the table is big enough, and if we roll up our sleeves and do the hard work of finding ways of representing all the relevant parameters, then we could actually get a gerrymandered object that really does have the right structure!

Second, you might think that a single static object can’t be conscious, but that there has to be some development over time. At the very least, signals have to travel between the neurons!

Fret not, as we can easily accommodate this! We simply define Tim to have a certain profile, not just in the spatial dimensions, but also across the time dimension. Suppose we represent signals with hexagons of cellulose molecules. We can then exactly mirror all the signals traveling in your brain in the table, by precisely defining the difference in locations of hexagons of cellulose across time in Tim.2 Likewise, we can make sure that neuronal connections, strengths of connections, etc., change over time!

IV.

Right okay, so if we had an object like Tim, it would be conscious. That’s fine, but all we have is a table… So much for that.

“No!” I scream, as I shake you vigorously “Remember your mereology lessons!!!” If you’re a universalist about composition—i.e. if you think that any combination of objects forms a further composite object—then there really exists an object like Tim in any sufficiently large table! In fact there exist extremely many (perhaps infinitely many), and nested and overlapping Tims. Consciousness galore!

So if you’re a type-type identity theorist of this sort, and a universalist, then you’ll have to say that there are all these consciousnesses. You’ll make regular panpsychists say “woah there, calm down!” with all the things you call conscious—all the intertwining and overlapping consciousnesses everywhere. Don’t let anyone tell you that mereology is a waste of time.

Or maybe do let them say that… The thing is, unless our theory of consciousness has a clause that says something like “and the conscious thing must be a real composite object,” then what we say about mereology doesn’t matter. Tim might not form a Composite Object™, but it still exists in some sense. And unless being a composite object is necessary for consciousness on the theory, that sense will have to be good enough.

V.

The title of this post was about functionalism, not about some random form of type-type identity theory, so when are we actually gonna get to functionalism? Now is when. As it happens, functionalism can be cashed out as a subset of the sort of theory that I’ve been talking about all this time. If we say that what individuates the types of physical states is their functional profiles, then that is just functionalism: To be a token pain is to be a token state that satisfies the functional profile of pain.

We immediately have to add an epicycle to the argument though. Functionalists will want to say that functions depend on causal relations. And while Tim might have the right spatiotemporal structure, that doesn’t mean that any causation is going on. This is right, and it will have to limit the scope of this argument to people with certain views about causation.

But if your name is (or was) David K. Lewis, then the argument certainly goes through. This is because what you say about causation is that A causes B iff B counterfactually depends on A—or in other words that in the closest world where A doesn’t obtain, B doesn’t obtain either. Not only that, you also say that the laws of composition are such that objects can have parts in different possible worlds (and you’re a universalist about composition).

This makes the argument trivially go through: Let’s consider a different part of the table—Laila—which will be isomorphic to some stimulus, such as some beam of light. We can then define Laila such that she exists in some possible worlds but not others. Similarly, we can have Tim exist in all the Laila-worlds, and then some. Not only that, but we can make sure that in all the Laila-worlds, Tim is in state A, but in all the closest non-Laila-worlds, Tim is in state B. If that’s right, then Laila causes Tim to be in state A—literally!

Again, it should be clear that this proof of concept could be scaled up to the actual causal profiles we need, if we were diligent enough. Since this is so, for a universalist, Tims and Lailas really do exist, and in huge numbers. And if you accept what I said about the irrelevance of mereology above, this is also true, regardless of your views in mereology.

More generally, it seems like if you’re some sort of Humean about causation, and if you think that objects in the relevant sense needed for the argument can be defined with specific modal profiles, then this argument goes through. Maybe it can be made to work on other combinations of views, but I’ll leave figuring that out as an exercise for the reader.

VI.

What does this argument show? Well, for one it only shows anything if we accept the assumptions (especially about causation) that it relies on. I don’t know how many functionalists do, but I’d assume that the number would be quite low, exactly for this kind of reason.

But supposing that the argument does go through, how bad is it? It’s certainly weird, but as the aforementioned Lewis has taught us all, an incredulous stare is no argument. Depending on your views about anthropics, we can get in trouble, though.

If you accept the SIA3 (as you should), this actually seems to make this theory quite likely. Among the Tims of the world will be many, many Tims in “brain states” exactly like your own (or arbitrarily close, at any rate). The SIA loves this, provided you construe evidence as only intrinsically depending on brain states. So the SIA gives a huge probability boost to Tim-allowing theories.

There’s also a flipside to the coin, however, as it would also seem to lead to radical skepticism. Most people with the same evidence as you will be Tims, meaning it’d be very likely that you are one—sort of like Boltzmann brains. Not only that, but the vast majority of Tims that are currently like you will have radically disorganized experiences the following moment. Hence you should not really trust induction, or anything for that matter. Scary.

On the other hand, if you accept the SSA,4 and think that the Tims would be in your reference class, then you get incredibly strong evidence against the combination of views that makes the argument here work. After all, most Tims will have very different evidence from you, so if they’re in your reference class, the SSA will tell you that these Tims most likely do not exist.

As for other views in anthropics, I’ll let you think about that for yourself.

On a final note, this argument really doesn’t hinge on physicalism at all. Say that a physicalist theory says that consciousness is identical to/constituted by/realized by/etc. physical states that satisfy C. Well, there will be a corresponding dualist theory that says that states that satisfy C cause the corresponding conscious experiences. In fact, the dualist and physicalist should probably agree quite closely about the neural correlates of consciousness (i.e. C), due to neuroscience.

More than 10 quadrillion consciousnesses believe that subscribing to Wonder and Aporia is the best thing you could do. That many people can’t be wrong!

You Might Also Like:

1

I’ve been told that this argument is very similar to (an instance of) triviality arguments against functionalism. So nothing new under the sun and all that. Though I’m not aware of a formulation like the one I give here.

2

Not that the same set of molecules literally moves inside the table, but that we include different molecules over time, such that the shape is realized by different molecules along the path over time.

3

The SIA is the view that you should reason as though you’re sampled from all possible observers. What this means in reality, is that a theory is more likely in proportion with how many more observers with the same evidence as you it predicts.

4

The SSA is the view that you should reason as though you’re sampled from all actual observers in your reference class. So theories which include many observers in your reference class that have different evidence from you will be correspondingly less likely.

item.title: Top 5 Reasons Why I'm No Longer Vegan
item.description: What they don't tell you at the grass-eaters' association
item.content:encoded:
I have previously argued for ethical veganism—i.e. that buying and eating animal products under ordinary circumstances is morally wrong. Recently, however, I have come to see the error of my ways. Since a lot of people on Substack are ethical vegans, I thought it would be fitting to own up to my mistakes here. Hopefully this can be of help to others who previously made the same mistakes as me.

1. Plant Agriculture Also Kills Animals

Unbeknownst to most, your bland old beetroot steak is only red because it’s soaked in the blood of the poor mice and birds that had to perish so you can sink your nasty teeth into it. Billions upon billions of animals die every year just so vegans can eat their “plants.” Frankly, I’m horrified that I could even touch that crap.

While the crooked plant-farmer casually mows over families of field mice and deer for sport, the animal-farmer gives us the nutrients straight from the source, no plants needed.

2. Vegans Want you to eat False Foods

Like many others, I’m cautious about the truth-value of what I put into my mouth. Needless to say it came as quite the shock to find out that vegan food is in large parts false. As Mike Parry has bravely pointed out, vegans surely wouldn’t want to eat false cabbage, would they? Why, then, are they asking others to eat foods which do not correspond to any facts? Preposterous!

If you don’t want to eat false foods yourself, then why ask that of others? I recommend that you only stick to the best-evidenced food you can find—and it goes without saying that that excludes all this vegan crap.1

3. Many People Have Traditions for Eating Meat

In my infinite stupidity, I had previously failed to consider the fact that many people around the world have traditions which involve eating meat. For instance eating ham for Christmas, lamb for Eid, or humans after sacrificing to the Aztec gods. If the problem this poses for veganism were not obvious already, let me make the inference explicit:

  1. There are traditions that involve eating meat.

  2. If something is involved in a tradition, it is logically impossible for it to be wrong.

  3. So eating meat is not wrong.

As we just discussed, premise (1) is established empirically. So since premise (2) is obvious even to the fool, as well as a transcendental condition for the possibility of reasoning itself, it follows that (3) is true.

4. You Can’t Have A Nutritious Diet As A Vegan

Now, this one came as a surprise for me. Until recently, I had been under the impression that I was alive and well. Imagine my shock when I found out that I had been dead for the longest time. Not only that, but some of the people I follow on here like and , as well as 9% of the population of India, have apparently been deceased for years. How BB has been able to posthumously pump out articles almost daily, and even get a new job is beyond me;2 but the facts don’t lie! You can’t have a nutritious diet as a vegan.

The worst offender is of course protein. Cabbage (regardless of truth-value) only has a puny 1.3g protein per 100g. If we round that to the nearest 2.7, that’s literally 0! As far as I know, cabbage is the only plant that exists, and so it follows logically that you can’t get protein on a vegan diet.

But even entertaining the counterpossible in which you manage to get any protein out of chewing rabbit food, you’re still dead meat. Humans need micronutrients such as B12, which are impossible to get on a vegan diet, as they are widely known only to spontaneously materialize inside cows. Sadly no one has ever thought of any way to get this without eating steaks. Rest in peace Bentham’s Bulldog; your articles on anthropics will be missed.

5. Lions Eat Meat

As a final nail in the coffin, I recently found out that not all animals are vegans. In fact, there are whole categories of animals that eat meat—so-called “omnivores” and “carnivores.” I can’t believe that no one had ever told me this. Just goes to show how deep this goes…

Anyways, while the vegan propaganda movie The Lion King made it seem like lions only eat grubs,3 turns out that they actually kill other animals to eat them.

You can only dream of the horror I felt the first time I saw a video of a lion munching away on the remains of a gazelle.

Now, this was of course a problem for me, as I—like most sane people—try to model my moral behavior as closely as I can on that of lions.

And since paying others to raise selectively bred genetic freaks in squalid conditions before slaughtering is the closest thing to beating down a gazelle with my bare hands I could think of, I saw no choice.

I will thus henceforth stop eating plants, constipation be damned—and I hope everyone reading this will follow my example.

Subscribe for the follow-up post where I explain how to live with scurvy.

1

Thanks to for making me aware of this brilliant argument. Ironic that a vegan himself would bring it to the attention of so many. Alas, such is often the folly of these “vegans.”

2

Connor’s recent output is sadly a little more explicable. :(

3

Which we all know are not real animals since they don’t have sclerae in cartoons, and hence don’t have souls.

item.title: Are Claims Evidence?
item.content:encoded:
Veteran counter-apologist Matt Dillahunty has recently been the object of a Discourse™ here on the platform, after Joe Schmidt (edit: Joe Schmid1 (edit edit: Jebediah Schmid) released a video in which he attempted to school Dillahunty in the epistemology of testimony. Dillahunty has been associated with his slogan:

Claims are not evidence!

Often in the context of debates about the resurrection. I think this slogan is strictly wrong, as well as more or less wrong in spirit (though it may have more merit when restricted to the context of adversarial debate). Here I’ll lay out what I think is the correct view about the epistemology of claims/testimony, and then build some levels of abstraction on this that make it simpler, which end out in the conclusion that the above is a bad heuristic.

I know that some parties to the discussion do not accept some of the background assumptions about epistemology I’ll be making here (thinking e.g. of ex-Joe ), but I’ll just explain my views and their motivations as clearly as possible, and then I hope it becomes clear why one would be compelled towards them. You can never hope to convince everyone!

More generally, I won’t go out of my way to explicitly address the Discourse in question, as I’ve honestly not been following it that closely. I just would like to explain what I believe to be the correct view, and that has some relevance for the dispute in question.

My Basic Thesis

The view that I think is correct is the following:

The General Thesis: Claims/testimony are evidence in exactly the same way as all other empirical evidence.

What I mean is that when I get the evidence that you claim “P,” what I’m really getting is strictly speaking the evidence that you made such and such movements with your mouth, such and such sounds, etc. That is then evidence about what you sincerely believe (generally that you believe P), and that is evidence about what sort of things you know, etc. etc.

It’s no different in kind from observing that a thermometer reads such and such temperature, and taking that as evidence that the room has a certain temperature.2 It’s just that humans are much more complicated than thermometers (or so I’ve heard), and so the connection is a lot less obvious.

Nevertheless, what happens is that I have some background credences about how likely it is that you make such and such claims given that you have made such and such observations or have such and such evidence. And I have background credences about how likely it is that the world is in this or that way given that you have these observations and evidence.

There is nothing magical that happens in testimony/claims compared to any other old kind of empirical observation. You just observe that something happens, and have some credences about what that means—it’s just that humans are pretty dang complex, and so the evidential import is much less obvious.

And importantly, there is no deep epistemic law about whether “S claims P” is evidence for P or not, anymore than there is any deep law about whether “this glass tube is this filled with red liquid” is evidence that the temperature of the room is some certain value. Depending on the glass tube, your background assumptions about what it’s like and how it works etc. it might be or it might not—and depending on the person, the context, what you know about them and about the topic, it might be evidence, it might not be, and it might even be evidence against.

One Layer of Abstraction: Evidence Aggregation

Okay, so that thesis is very plausible to me! But it’s also not particularly helpful, just like saying “believe what is true” or “do what is right” doesn’t really help much when it’s not at all obvious what is true or right.

So while The General Thesis is the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth—the final word if you just want to know the abstract description of the correct view—we still need some mid-level principles that are more useful approximations.

For this I think the view that develops in his excellent book Normative Externalism (specifically chapter 12) does quite well. He defends what he calls the “evidence aggregation” theory of disagreement.

You might now wonder: “Huh, I thought we were talking about testimony/claims. Why are we now talking about disagreement?” Well, certain views might want to treat these two differently, but we can count disagreement as a special case of testimony—specifically the cases where the content of the testimony is simply the negation of the hypothesis under consideration (or the testifier’s belief in that negation). In testimony the question is often about the sincerity of the testifier, whereas in disagreement this is generally not under dispute. Still, the underlying epistemology of what’s going on is basically the same, as we’ll see.

In the chapter in question, Weatherson spends a lot of time on the minutiae of the dialectic between his view and conciliations about disagreement. Most of that isn’t too important for us. But his statement of the view in the start fits very nicely into what we’re talking about here:

I defend a view that I’ll call the evidence aggregation theory of disagreement. When someone hears that a peer disagrees with them, that is defeasible evidence the peer has evidence that they lack. Ideally, the hearer would work out exactly what that evidence is, add it to their stock of evidence, and react accordingly. That ideal is rarely, if ever, realised. In more realistic cases, the hearer assigns different probabilities to different hypotheses about what may have produced the disagreement. The typical case is that the peer has reacted differently to having different evidence to the hearer. And it is also typical that that’s because the peer has evidence that the hearer lacks. So in (most) typical cases, the hearer will think there is evidence that they lack which supports the peer’s view, and typically the rational reaction to learning that is to move one’s views in the direction of the peer’s view. But this credal movement is defeasible thrice over; sometimes the hearer knows the peer has reacted irrationally, sometimes the hearer knows the peer has strictly less evidence than they do, and (in very rare cases) the rational reaction to evidence of evidence for a rival view is not to move one’s view towards the rival view.

Once we apply this to testimony, it is more or less just a way of drawing out the details of how the update mandated by The General Thesis is usually done: The evidential weight of the fact that someone makes a certain claim is that there are general tendencies for people to make those claims when they believe it—and importantly when they have some sort of reason (or evidence) for believing it.

You can come up with contrived counterexamples where the fact that someone makes a certain claim has evidential value outside of the fact that it’s evidence that they have some evidence. E.g.:

You and your spy-friend James—Bond James—are out on a mission at a party. For secret spy-reasons, James has to convey whether some door is locked or not to you. For further even cooler spy-reasons, you cannot talk openly about this—in fact, you can’t talk directly at all.

Instead the plan is this: If the door is locked, James will tell the friendly small-talker Ruth that he had toast for breakfast, and if it isn’t, he’ll tell her that he had chia pudding. Being an eager smalltalker, she’ll almost surely convey this to you.

It’s the night of the mission, and you go up to Ruth who tells you “oh, wouldn’t you know, Bond James just told me that he had chia pudding for breakfast. How curious!”

Okay, that was a long case to demonstrate a simple result: In this case the claim “Bond James had chia pudding” is evidence that the door is unlocked. This is not because Ruth has some evidence pertaining to the door that you didn’t. Hence this shows that evidence aggregation is not exhaustively what goes on epistemically with claims.

This is no problem because the ground truth is The General Thesis, and evidence aggregation is just more specific description of what the epistemic value of claims usually consist in.

With this pedantic aside, let’s look at a few examples, and how evidence aggregation handles them:

Ordinary Football: It’s an ordinary day in an ordinary situation—nothing out of the ordinary. Sandy, your perfectly ordinary friend, comes up to you and says “hey, I just bought a new football.”

What should this do to your beliefs? I think it’s totally blindingly obvious that this should make you quite confident that she did, in fact, buy a new football. Evidence aggregation tells us why: The fact that she made the claim is good evidence that she has some evidence in favor of her buying the football (e.g. remembering that she did do so). And if you add that evidence to your own stock of evidence, you should become a lot more confident that she did.

Let me now make a stipulation (we’ll come around to this move again below): By “evidence for P” I mean positive relevance. That is, E is evidence for P iff learning E should make you more confident in P.3 According to this definition, the claim that Sandy makes is thus evidence for the content of her claim.

Suspicious Football: It’s a very mysterious and off-feeling day—something’s not right here. Sandy, your all-round sketchy friend who’s notoriously unreliable about all things concerning footballs, comes up to you with a sly smile and says “hey… *wink wink*, you know I tooootally just bought a new football
*wink wink, nudge nudge*.”

In this case, the fact that Sandy makes the claim is not particularly strong reason that she has evidence that supports her buying a football. Given the context and detail, it is quite likely that she would make the claim whether or not she remembers having bought a football. So you shouldn’t think that she has that evidence, and so you shouldn’t add it to your stock of evidence. So in turn the claim is not evidence for its content.

In fact, it might be positive evidence against its content. Suppose that you were already sort of 50/50 about whether she’d buy a football (maybe she previously sincerely told you that she was considering it). Her saying the above in that situation is plausibly more likely if she didn’t buy a football than if she did. Hence it is evidence that she does not remember buying a football, and so evidence that she didn’t.

Rumor: Sandy tells you that Mike told her that Tina told him that Joey shat his pants yesterday. Now, as it happened you were in the room with Joey and Tina yesterday, when Joey farted very loudly. Tina immediately ran out towards Mike. You, the true friend you are, stayed with Joey and helpfully checked his underpants, where you saw that it was all air, no fluid—all bark, no bite.

In this case Sandy’s claim is no evidence for the content of her claim. It is evidence that she has the evidence “Mike told me that Tina told me that Joey shat his pants”. This is something you didn’t already know, and you add it to your evidence. But adding it to your evidence doesn’t change anything, as you have more specific evidence that screens off the evidential weight of the evidence Sandy has with regards to whether or not Joey shat his pants.

Delusion: Your kindly grandmother Sandy has been getting a little kooky lately, and has been diagnosed with “Napoleon syndrome” in which she routinely comes to believe that she is Napoleon Bonaparte. One day she says “I once lost a battle at Waterloo.”

In this case, the claim is not evidence. The claim is evidence that she has the evidence of remembering that she lost a battle of Waterloo. But once you add “Sandy remembers losing a battle at Waterloo” to your evidence, your confidence in that claim shouldn’t rise much, due to your background knowledge.

Okay, so I’ve just spent a lot of time giving examples where claims fail to be evidence. This illustrates the basic point that there is no deep law about the evidential weight of claims—it’s just like all other kinds of evidence, if only harder to evaluate due to the complexity of humans. So you can point to plenty of examples where claims fail to be evidence.

But I also want to make something clear: Most cases are like Ordinary Football. In most cases people assert what they believe, they have some sort of evidence for their belief, and you have no special reason that defeats the evidence you get from their claims.

Another Layer: Claims Are (Presumptively) Evidence

This last point is very important! Almost all claims are evidence (of varying quality). There are plenty of cases like Suspicious Football, Rumor, and Delusion, but in most cases some claim is presumptive evidence for the content of that claim.

The evidence aggregation view is still pretty complicated, so to aid our epistemic lives, we may wish to search for a yet more easily applicable heuristic. I suggest:

Claims are (presumptively) evidence.

The keen reader may notice that this almost perfectly contradicts the original slogan we considered. The “claims aren’t evidence” slogan is, of course, ambiguous between several readings. For example:4

  1. There are no claims that are evidence.

  2. Not all claims are evidence.

  3. Claims are generally not evidence.

  4. The property of being a claim is not the same as (or cointensional with) the property of being evidence.

  5. …

Some of these are fine (and quite trivial), such as (2) and (4). Some are obviously wrong as demonstrated by Ordinary Football, such as (1). And some are harder to evaluate, such as (3). But I think that the interesting interpretations (like (3)) will generally be false, for the reason I have just pointed out: In our world it happens that the norms around assertion, belief, etc., are such that claims are usually evidence, unless you have special reason to think otherwise.5

The “claims are not evidence” slogan is a poor candidate for a ground level truth about epistemology on par with The General Thesis. But plausibly it’s also not an attempt to express such a truth. Rather it’s supposed to be a very general heuristic. Sadly it is also a bad heuristic, as claims really are generally evidence in our world, even if you can come up with a lot of examples where they aren’t. The better heuristic (I claim) is:

Claims are (presumptively) evidence.

Sidenote: There may be contexts in which Dillahunty’s slogan is more appropriate. For example, I think it’s a plausible enough heuristic that “bare assertions in adversarial or contested contexts are not evidence.” In a debate it’s a good norm that you back up assertions with further evidence—and usually people are not unsure about what your view on the matter in question is. So the heuristic is fine here.

The worry I have is when heuristics like this overgeneralize and become reified as genuine principles in epistemology. It is not! The General Principle is the correct view, evidence aggregation is very close, and this heuristic is very defeasible and restricted. I think that people like Matt (and very much apologists too, for that matter) tend to be quick to make this sort of reification, where they confuse the heuristic for the principle, making them impervious to more nuanced discussion about the cases where the heuristic might come into question. And that’s very frustrating.

How Deep Does the Evidence Go?

Now, at this point you might be tempted to say that, “okay, fine, you should often rationally increase your confidence in the content of someone’s claim, all else being equal. But the claim is still not evidence for the claim.”

The idea, I take it, would be that there is a difference between evidence that directly pertains to some hypothesis (“real” evidence)—e.g. seeing Jones kill Smith with your own two eyes as direct evidence that Jones killed Smith—and claims that support some hypothesis indirectly—e.g. hearing Baker say that she saw Jones kill Smith.

I think we’re well in semantic-dispute territory here. If you agreed with everything I said thus far, you should agree with me on all matters about how claims affect your rational degrees of belief. As for the further claim of what is evidence and what is not, that’s neither here nor there. It’s just a matter of how we define the word “evidence” and nothing productive will come from disputing it.

Still—in a small performative contradiction—let me give some reason for why I would generally prefer a permissive idea of evidence (such as some sort of positive relevance definition).

First, you’re gonna have trouble cleanly dividing up the levels of evidence, it seems. Often what we count as “direct” evidence is really based on a bunch in inferences already. For instance, if I see a spectrometer spit out a certain absorption spectrum matching that of Red 40, I got evidence that the sample contains Red 40.

But really, this is only evidence given some background about what the absorption spectrum of Red 40 is, how a spectrometer works, that it is not defective, etc. And on certain paths down the line of assumptions might be ones based on claims/testimony.6 Maybe my friend told me that “yeah this is definitely a spectrometer, and not a schmecschrometer that is consistently biased in the direction of Red 40.”

Obviously a contrived example, but the point should be clear enough: Claims can lurk everywhere in the evidential ancestry of your beliefs, so it is very hard to make a sharp distinction between “direct” evidence and evidence based on claims. So theoretically, my definition is neat and clean.

In fact, scientific practice is in large part based on testimony. This is an issue that has shown up a couple of times in the discussion as well, and been disputed. I assume the dispute is mostly verbal, as the “ground level facts” seem pretty clear to me: Most people have not personally witnessed the experiments that confirm the scientific results we believe in. Instead the results have been relayed by some people in a report, and people take this at face value. So they take the claims in the report as evidence for the truth of the content of those claims (due to the background assumptions about the sincerity of scientists).

Now, it’s true that science doesn’t ultimately bottom out in claims. Someone has to actually do the experiments at some point! But most of most people’s knowledge about science are the result of other’s claims/testimony.

Second, I worry that being a “snob” about evidence might risk devaluing rational considerations that don’t fall under the category of “evidence.” This is basically along the lines of what I expressed in the sidenote previously. If we think of claims as a separate inferior type of evidence than other sorts of evidence, we risk discounting it when we shouldn’t.

There is of course also the risk in the other direction of thinking that claims are stronger evidence than they are, since we put them on a par with other types. So it’s a balancing act.

Conclusion

In conclusion, I’m right and you’re wrong.

Or in a little more detail, The General Thesis seems clearly correct to me! The evidence aggregation view is a very good way of cashing this out. And “claims are presumptively evidence” is in many cases a good heuristic approximation of this.

I suspect that almost all of the disagreement is (or should be), about this last step (about what heuristic is correct), or verbal disputes about what “claims” and “evidence” mean.

By “evidence” I have meant positive relevance. You can define it otherwise, but that doesn’t change the substance of what I say. If you agree with me when we hold the definition of “evidence” fixed, then there’s nothing to disagree about.

Similarly, I worry that people might be confusing what they mean with “claim”: Obviously free-floating sentence-types are not evidence. That doesn’t even make sense! The sentence “I ate PB&J for breakfast” in the abstract isn’t evidence. What can be evidence are particular assertions of sentences by particular people.

Once we hold these things fixed, I hope that the actual substance of the epistemic principles should be more or less uncontroversial (though there might be disagreements on the margins). You might disagree what is the better heuristic principle, but at that point we’re no longer talking epistemology, but about what as a matter of fact is the most useful thing to believe—and in that case we shouldn’t get caught up in ostensibly epistemic debates.

I claim that you should subscribe to Wonder and Aporia.
